title: A Privacy Company Just Saved the Clearest Flock Surveillance Map I’ve Seen
snippet: The creator of Proton Mail now hosts a powerful, professional Flock camera mapping tool on its site.
fullText:
A powerful, free Flock surveillance-tracking platform is now hosted by Proton, the creator of Proton Mail and Proton VPN. The move provides extra technical and legal protection for the interactive mapping tool, which Flock has repeatedly attempted to shut down through legal threats.

The deal, announced on Wednesday, gives the public access to a free database of Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and AI surveillance cameras across the US.

Security researcher Joshua Michael first published the interactive map in September before facing a swift trademark complaint from Flock. Despite Flock’s demands for its removal, the map remains publicly accessible.

			

More from CNET

Flock’s surveillance networks capture license plates, vehicle details, human physical characteristics, and audio signals such as gunshots or shouting. While law enforcement agencies use this data to track and search suspects, privacy advocates warn that the technology enables widespread, unchecked tracking.

Proton also says the map shows far more Flock cameras are active than Flock currently says it has. Flock said this summer that it operates more than 120,000 cameras nationwide, but the tool says there are more than 214,000 Flock devices in service, with more than 80,000 in the planning stages. 

A representative from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The map is one of the most usable Flock tools I’ve seen. Proton’s Flock tool has better visual clarity, faster search responses and a more intuitive interface than other sites I’ve tried and is available without a subscription to other Proton services.

I searched my own city, which canceled its Flock contact over a year ago. The map accurately reported that no active Flock cameras are currently present, but correctly located decommissioned Flock cams. Since the data is based on Flock’s own reporting, I place more trust in it than in crowdsourced tools like the Deflock app, which are subject to errors or misrepresentation.

Proton’s tool is striking to look at and simple to use.Proton

“My research on FlockSurveillance.org documents cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences,” map creator Joshua Michael told CNET. “My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people.”

Michael said Flock has “promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline,” he said, offering that as one reason why Proton moved to preserve the map in its Swiss servers. Switzerland enforces some of the world’s strongest privacy laws. Proton’s site notes that under Swiss data protection regulations, the company isn’t required to comply with requests that are not supported by a Swiss court order. Flock is a US-based company.

Camera locations are constantly changing, meaning a surveillance map could rapidly become dated.

“If new and reliable data becomes available, then we will update the map,” a Proton spokesperson told me. “We’re committed to keeping the public informed of all forms of surveillance where reliable data can be sourced.” 

Another surveillance mapping option

While Proton’s map provides a specialized, point-in-time look at Flock Safety’s network, the Atlas of Surveillance offers a broader, historical catalog of the sweeping technologies US law enforcement agencies have quietly adopted over the years. 

Powered by a network of volunteers who analyze public data and official government records, the Atlas database tracks everything from automated license plate readers to cell-site simulators and body-worn cameras. The project continuously updates its findings.

fullText:
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.

Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.

1/5An image generated by Canva Craft. Image: Canva

The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.

Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.

Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
snippet: The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts.
fullText:
Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. 

Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.

The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents, accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.

1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.

“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post. “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”

Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.

This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.

Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

title: Anthropic Introduces Claude Duet: A New Agentic AI App for Professionals
snippet: It’s nothing we haven’t seen before, but it’s hyper specificity toward business owners and professionals.
fullText:
Anthropic is dropping yet another AI product into our laps: Claude Duet, a dedicated app for professionals and business owners to handle tasks they would otherwise have to do manually. While agentic AI isn’t new, this app caters to a group that likely needs those capabilities most. Anthropic has always targeted the professional sector, and Duet, while specific, feels very on-brand for the company.

Claude Duet is designed around Opus 5.5, and the app is aimed at streamlining your daily operations. Not unlike Claude itself, Duet allows you to connect with the software you use for your work, and will continuously look for things that need your attention. This means you can connect your Gmail, calendar, Slack and thousands of other work and productivity apps. 

Like other agentic tools, Duet is a proactive assistant that will help you prioritize things that it deems are most important and worthy of your attention first. The “proactive” part of Duet is that you don’t always have to prompt it to do something for the future; it’ll assess and assemble what you need to know by looking through your work apps. It’ll also do the opposite, and tell you when things can wait for later so you can focus on higher-priority tasks. 

			

More from CNET

Anthropic says that Claude Duet prioritizes your privacy. As much as an AI tool can, at least. There are specialized safety protocols and measures to make sure sensitive information doesn’t go out into the world unless you want it to. Duet will automatically reject highly sensitive information, like credit card numbers, ID information and more. With other sensitive information, like health and finance information, Duet will ask before it sends anything out. 

Duet is currently available in a research preview, but only for the Pro or Max subscription plans. You can join the waitlist now.

title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions
snippet: Third Dimension's technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian's reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.
fullText:
EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview.

Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles.

Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over. 

Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028.

“The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.”

Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap.

Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator. 

“For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.” 

It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.”

Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable.

Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1T pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day.

Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said.

“Especially when you think about validation, right? So that’s really the piece where you’re saying, ‘is the system good to ship?’” Philbin said. “And there, you really want to have a good sense of this sim-to-real gap, because to do that kind of hand on heart, you really need to trust that answer is in the positive. Otherwise, you’re measuring something that’s not representative of how it will actually perform in the real world.”

This article was updated to include more quotes from Philbin and more details on Rivian’s automated driving strategy.

title: INMO GO3 smart glasses pack a display and Gemini integration with clever camera privacy
snippet: There are two problems with smart glasses today. Most don’t deliver that futuristic display we all want to have, and the camera has become a serious point of friction. INMO GO3 solve both problems while also supporting Google’s Gemini and more. more…
fullText:
There are two problems with smart glasses today. Most don’t deliver that futuristic display we all want to have, and the camera has become a serious point of friction. INMO GO3 solve both problems while also supporting Google’s Gemini and more.

The promise of INMO GO3 is to deliver an AI-forward pair of smart glasses that help you stay connected and get things done, but without using your phone quite as much. It delivers on that through software, of course, but also the fact that it puts an actual display in front of your eyes. So, unlike most existing smart glasses, you’re able to interact with everything without interrupting a conversation or glancing at your phone. The MicroLED displays – one for each eye – are bright (up to 1,500 nits) and have a 30-degree field-of-view.

One of the core features is translation, with GO3 supporting real-time translation across 98 languages, and even supporting 13 languages fully offline. The glasses detect speech from the person in front of you and put a translation of that right in your eyeline, letting you get over the language barrier without putting your phone in the middle. Similarly, GO3 can take notes during meetings, and coming soon, it will also be able to present summaries directly through the glasses.

The display can also be used as a teleprompter, or to interact with an AI assistant. INMO’s AI assistant is powered by Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT and can do things such as answer questions, recognize images taken by the camera, and take notes, among other functions. The display can also be used for turn-by-turn navigation to help you get around without using your phone.

	

Despite all the additional functionality here, INMO GO3 remain lightweight. The glasses weigh in at 58g, just a tiny bit heavier than Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses – the ones without a display. The 8mm temples also ensure these don’t stand out in a bad way – they just look like normal glasses!

One of the coolest features here is the battery. Smart glasses by their very nature are limited in terms of how long the battery can go, so INMO designed the battery to be interchangeable. When the first battery drains, simply swap out the power pack with a fresh one that’s on the charger and keep wearing the glasses. The included charging case can still top off the battery, but a replaceable cell gets you up and going faster.

As mentioned, there is a camera on board here, but one of the really thoughtful additions INMO offers is a privacy cover. This physical shade covers the camera lens, providing some visible confirmation that the camera is not in use.

INMO GO3 also gets some boosts from accessories such as a speaker that can be used alongside AI translation to respond to the other person in their language, but using an AI clone of your voice. There’s also a controller ring you can wear to interact with GO3’s software without touching the actual glasses. Finally, you can also add on a sunglasses cover to improve GO3’s usability outside, and there are prescription lens inserts too.

INMO GO3 is on sale now for just $509.

title: Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers
snippet: Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation. more…
fullText:
Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation.

Free trials are a pretty standard practice across the industry when it comes to subscriptions, and the general understanding is that you’re getting full access to the same subscription you are later set to pay for unless there’s an upfront stipulation about restrictions.

And that’s where things are getting a bit messy with Google’s AI Pro subscription.

Google One AI Pro is a $19.99/month subscription that delivers access to expanded Gemini usage limits, 5TB of storage across Google products, and bundles in other subscriptions such as Google Home Premium, Health Premium, and YouTube Premium Lite. Earlier this year, we called AI Pro “one of the best deals in tech today.”

	

But the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon to Google’s Antigravity development tool put a spotlight on a restriction on AI Pro’s free trials. Put simply, they’re limited compared to paid subscribers, and it’s not something Google made abundantly clear.

There are two specific downsides with a Google One AI Pro trial compared to an actively paid subscription. As mentioned, Antigravity on AI Pro trials leaves out Gemini 4 Argon. Google has a page that specifically puts a trial account in a completely different bucket compared to a paid AI Pro plan, and it treats the trial as a free user with expanded usage limits rather than a full user as @evowizz was one of the first to point out.

The other restriction is YouTube Premium Lite, which is not available for Google One AI Pro trial users until they start paying.

In Google’s defense, this is technically spelled out on support documents. The YouTube Premium Lite restriction, for example, is clearly spelled out as Google says that the “benefit is unavailable until trials of Google AI Pro conclude and you convert to a paid subscription.” But, as far as we can see, this is not disclosed as clearly at the time of sign-up or alongside advertising of the AI Pro trials.

Another loss here is the lack of Google One’s 10% cashback (store credit) perk in the Google Store, which is lacking in free trials. That one is certainly easier to see the reasoning behind, though.

The Google Store touts the Pixel 11’s AI Pro trial as delivering “expanded usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini in Google apps, and 5 TB of cloud storage,” as well as Health Premium. Nowhere does Google promise the YouTube perks, but the wording around Gemini also lacks any hint at the restriction found in Antigravity. Pages including offer details also lack any mention of this.

As mentioned, Google hands out free, extended trials to AI Pro all over the place. Just a few active examples include:

6 months free with the purchase of a Pixel 11

12 months free with the purchase of a Googlebook

6 months free for select Verizon customers

12 months free with Chromebook Plus or 3 months with any other Chromebook

6 months free with the purchase of a Galaxy Z Fold 8

And that’s just a few examples – you can absolutely find more.

	

Google explicitly lists all of these trials at their full monthly value (i.e. $119 value for Pixel’s 6-month trial) despite the restricted access that trial users see.

While Google has not addressed the somewhat misleading nature of the AI Pro trial restrictions, one Googler responded to the other headache that exists here – you can’t just press a button to start paying for AI Pro if you’re on a trial. You either have to wait for the trial to end, or reach out to Google for help converting your account. 

What do you think of the situation?

title: I Tried Automating My Relationships Using AI Agents. Muse and Dots Overstepped
snippet: If it takes more time to review and approve a simple email than it would for me to write it myself, the whole promise of agentic AI falls flat.
fullText:
Most people revel in milestones. Turning the yearly page on birthdays, holidays and anniversaries is an opportunity for big parties, exchanging nice gifts and celebrating the ones we love. It can also be a minefield of missed connections and hurt feelings if you forget the dates.

If you’re ever sent a “happy belated birthday” message, neglected to recall your own anniversary or simply struggle to keep in touch with people, this guide might be for you. Granted, you’ll have to put your trust in an AI agent to do the heavy lifting, but you might never need to remember to send a card again.

While AI may not understand human connection and happiness, what it does well with is rote tasks. I tried to use ChatGPT and a few other AI tools to automate the upkeep of my personal and professional relationships — but here’s where it all went wrong.

			

More from CNET

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

‘Happy belated birthday,’ no more?

The penalties for being terrible at remembering birthdays increase as one gets older. Soon it’s not just your friend’s birthdays that slip your mind, but also their kids’ birthdays and your grandkids’ birthdays and on and on as the wheel of reproduction turns. 

I used ChatGPT — which appeared to be the only AI tool among the three I tested that could automate this entire process for me — to identify key birthdays of friends and family and develop an automation system to make sure I never miss another important date. 

Claude was able to access and draft emails as well as create birthday cards and greetings, but not automate the sending.

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini seemed like it could only work with me in the chat to draft emails and generate custom cards, not actually work inside my inbox. Only some people have access to Google’s AI agent, Gemini Spark, right now.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

I authorized ChatGPT and its agentic offering, Dots, to look through my Google Calendar and Gmail to find and match dates to the birthdays of the people most important to me. You can do this by navigating to your profile icon in ChatGPT, clicking Settings and then opening Plugins.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

I also gave ChatGPT authorization to read, compose and send emails on my behalf. 

Then I asked ChatGPT to look through my calendar and Gmail and find as many important birthdays as it could.

ChatGPT correctly analyzed my inbox and discovered a great deal about the birthdays, personal habits and interests of my loved ones. (Surnames and birthdays redacted for privacy.)ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT was able to use my inbox to boil down my friends’ and family’s interests to a broad, yet specific, enough set of data points to create custom digital birthday cards that actually fit all their personalities. Even the one friend ChatGPT know much about still got a digital card that fit her pretty much to a T.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

Automating all my love

Now comes the most crucial element — setting up ChatGPT to automatically send digital birthday cards and greetings to all the important people in my life so I don’t screw it up. I tested this feature by asking ChatGPT to generate a digital card and message for my dog’s birthday and send the email to my husband.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

The chat limit was reached here, and ChatGPT also surfaced an alert that asked for my permission to send an email on my behalf. And while it can be good in general for an AI agent to ask for your permission before sending an email, I had tasked it with sending those specific emails by itself automatically each time.

Beyond my email task, I also asked Meta Muse, the social media giant’s AI agent, to send memes and check-ins to a few of my friends on Instagram. This ended up being more trouble than it was worth; the content Muse selected to send along was based on seemingly nothing specific, just random posts sourced from around the platform that might be construed as mildly amusing. 

The bottom line on AI agents overstepping

This is where things get a little fuzzy. The amount of work it took to optimize Dots and Muse so they would send relevant, plausibly functional correspondence was not worth it. If it takes more time to review, revise and approve a simple email or DM than it would for me to do it myself, the whole prospect and promise of agentic AI falls flat.  

Ultimately, you should also be aware that once you’re working with an AI agent, it may also start to overstep in the chat. I had to tell both Muse and ChatGPT’s Dots to back off — because while I’d given them permission to peruse my emails and social media accounts, I had only asked them to complete certain, very specific, actions while doing it.

ChatGPT/Meta/Screenshot by CNET

Dot took it upon itself, totally unprompted, to alert me to a timing snag in my evening, going through my emails and letting me know a movie I’d bought tickets for conflicted with my Japanese class that night. This might have been useful, had I not already sent an email to my teacher right after buying the tickets, letting them know I’d be missing class.

Muse started sending me unsolicited updates about the weather and a fire in Malibu. Both undertook relentless efforts to get me to use more and more of their features while I had the apps active. 

Overall, the experience didn’t leave me feeling more connected to anything but the AI companies.
excerpt:
Most people revel in milestones. Turning the yearly page on birthdays, holidays and anniversaries is an opportunity for big parties, exchanging nice gifts and celebrating the ones we love. It can also be a minefield of missed connections and hurt feelings if you forget the dates.

If you’re ever sent a “happy belated birthday” message, neglected to recall your own anniversary or simply struggle to keep in touch with people, this guide might be for you. Granted, you’ll have to put your trust in an AI agent to do the heavy lifting, but you might never need to remember to send a card again.

title: The Mori Is a Mushroom-Shaped AI Lamp Companion, and I’m Smitten
snippet: The $849 Mori is designed to respond to your environment, knowing when to play and when to stay quiet.
fullText:
So many artificial intelligence devices are trying to command our attention, but when I met the Mori AI robot companion earlier this month, it was refreshing to see a device that’s using AI to exercise some playful restraint — even if its $849 retail price makes it a tough sell.

The Mori, announced Thursday by its maker Oka, is part glowy mushroom lamp and part Furby. And while it also looks a little bit like a larger smart speaker wrapped in fabric, the cutesy AI gadget made it quite clear that it was not interested in playing any of my playlists from Apple Music.

Mori listens to music here, and then hides after becoming shy.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Instead, when activated, the Mori pops out of its body and uses its cameras and sensors to respond playfully to you — and, like a Furby, it speaks its own babylike language. It’s 10 inches tall (26.4 centimeters) and uses its sensors to help it tilt its head and move its “eyes” to follow your voice. Oka says the Mori processes images and audio on the device to discern context, then discards them. The device does store facial recognition data to distinguish familiar faces from unfamiliar ones, but Oka says that data isn’t uploaded either.

			

More from CNET

When I spoke directly to the Mori during my demo, it felt a lot like speaking to a friend’s dog: It will look and respond, but also reacts to other things at the same time. The AI that it uses to understand context seemed to come into play when I commented on how adorable it looked (it cooed and got a little shy) and when I asked Oka CEO Hua Wang if the Mori had a Bluetooth mode for playing music (the gadget made a sound of disapproval).

When withdrawn into its body, Mori turns off its cameras, plays meditative music and becomes a colorful lamp.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The Mori does play music, though its offerings are limited to meditative sounds accompanied by a glowing light show. Press its head, and it retreats into its body to play white noise-like songs while its head lights up in a variety of colors. It also reacts to music: It started bopping around when I played Carly Rae Jepsen’s Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.

The adorable yet understated personality reminds me of the Furby from yesteryear and the $599 Ultimate Grogu we saw earlier this year, but the Mori’s use of AI allows it to react more contextually to its surroundings. This more docile take on a pet could appeal to someone who wants something more responsive than a talking toy that also blends in with their living room furniture.

To show it’s paying attention, Mori’s head tilts towards your voice and its eyes can follow you around.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The Mori costs more than those toys: $649 for its founder edition, $799 for the next round of preorders and, eventually, $849 for its standard edition. However, it’s a lot more affordable than a companion robot such as Sony’s $3,200 Aibo robot dog. It comes bundled with two years of its subscription, and afterward will cost either $17 per month or $80 per year.

Oka calls this edition the “Artificat 01” and intends for it to develop its personality as it lives with its owner. If an “Artificat 02” comes along down the road, your Mori’s personality should be able to transfer to its new body.

While I do think the Mori is adorable, it’s worth noting that companion robots already come in a lot of different forms, and we’ll likely see even more this January at CES 2027. These include robots that can float in the air and those designed as assistants and social companions for older adults. Oka appears to be taking a gentler approach, with a look that could fit right in alongside living room or bedroom furniture.

title: OpenAI GPT models are coming to Google Antigravity ‘soon,’ Cloud ‘in the coming weeks’
snippet: A deal struck between OpenAI and Google will see OpenAI’s models coming to Google Cloud and even Antigravity. more…
fullText:
A deal struck between OpenAI and Google will see OpenAI’s models coming to Google Cloud and even Antigravity.

Starting “in the coming weeks,” OpenAI’s GPT models will be coming to Google Cloud. OpenAI says that “Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via the model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace.” This enables enterprise customers with “spend commitments” through Google Cloud to use OpenAI’s models if they choose. 

The Google Cloud model garden already supports Anthropic Claude models alongside open models and Google’s own Gemini models. 

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, says:

	

We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs.

Also confirmed in today’s announcement is that OpenAI models are coming to Google’s Antigravity tool, as well as Gemini Agent.

Like Cloud’s model garden, Antigravity already supports Anthropic models including Claude Opus & Sonnet 4.6 for free/Plus/trial accounts (until November 2), with Opus & Sonnet 5.5 models available to paid subscribers on Pro and higher tiers. 

OpenAI and Google have yet to confirm exactly which GPT models will be coming to Cloud and Antigravity, but it stands to reason that GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol may be included.

title: Americans Say Rising Utility Costs Are Straining Their Budgets. They’re Blaming Data Centers
snippet: 1 in 5 households have cut back on groceries because of energy bills, according to a new Consumer Reports survey.
fullText:
There’s a reason Americans have cited energy costs as one of the biggest issues on their minds during this year’s elections: A new survey by Consumer Reports found that, among Americans who’ve lived in the same home for more than three years, the vast majority are paying more for energy now than three years ago — and it’s affecting their budgets.

Three out of four surveyed families reported that the utility rate increases have resulted in strained household finances. Over a quarter of these US customers said their bills rose by 20 to 49%, while 6% of respondents reported rate hikes of over 50% in the past three years. Electricity rates have risen dramatically in recent years.

People are increasingly choosing between necessities as purse strings tighten. 

			

More from CNET

One in four families chose to adjust the thermostat to uncomfortable levels in the summer and winter. Other folks are choosing to cut back on non-essential spending, like eating out and traveling. In the most dire cases, Americans are choosing to slash grocery budgets. About 20% of people surveyed told Consumer Reports that they’re buying less food or are switching to less expensive options.

The two largest factors that ratepayers attributed their increased electricity bills to are utility company profits and AI infrastructure. As data centers continue to proliferate across the country, over 75% of people surveyed said they don’t trust their state lawmakers to protect them against rate increases.

Across the political spectrum, the vast majority of US voters oppose AI data center construction in their backyard. These facilities contribute to rising electricity costs, local water contamination and fossil fuel pollution. While supporters argue that constructing and operating data centers creates new jobs, critics say these economic benefits are temporary and have a limited impact on the local community.

When asked about potential solutions, most Americans pointed in the same direction: More regulation for AI data center owners, utility companies and appliance manufacturers.

More than 80% of people surveyed said that utility companies should create a separate rate category for data center-sized users while 50% of respondents said they think it’s unacceptable for utility companies to pass on expenses to residential customers through higher rates.

But the levers to make any of those changes remain in your lawmakers’ hands, so the question remains: What can you personally do to save on your electricity bills?

Before you reach for the thermostat, see if this advice can help you tamp down that electricity bill.Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Energy-efficient appliances can help — a bit

You may not have much direct control over how much a kilowatt-hour of electricity costs, but you have some say in how many kilowatt-hours you use. Taking a close look at your home’s energy efficiency could save you, at least a little bit.

Energy-efficient appliances will also help you complete the same household tasks for a much lower cost. While President Trump’s administration has threatened to axe the Energy Star program, the government initiative is still kicking and can help you save money while hunting for anything from new refrigerators to smart plugs and thermostats.

Energy Star labels are proof that a product meets certain efficiency standards. The official Energy Star website allows you to search through different categories to find accredited products that you need.

If you aren’t in the market for a new appliance (or you’re a renter with less agency over your living space), there are some seasonal energy-saving lifehacks that can still save you a pretty penny.

As winter arrives at our doorstep, you’ve got a balancing act between limiting your energy consumption and staying comfortable. The easiest way to keep the heating bill down is to insulate your home, preventing some of that chill from seeping in to start with. And keeping key areas insulated, like your water pipes, will also retain precious heat and save electricity there (while keeping pipes from freezing and breaking). If your utility usage is still too high, we have other winter tips you can turn to instead.

There are also tons of year-round tips you can practice for free. Completely turning off electronics instead of leaving them in sleep mode, ensuring you turn off the lights when you leave a room and moving your thermostat to the right place are just some of the dozens of easy ways you can consciously save money. You don’t even have to follow all of these tips – picking and choosing a couple of the easiest ones will stack up some quick savings.

Of course, if you’re still trying to figure out what your bill means, Consumer Reports also debuted a new bill decoder tool to figure out what’s driving up your utility bills and advocate for yourself. The free site allows you to upload your bills to break down confusing pricing information before offering access to any money-saving resources or programs near you. It also helps Consumer Reports track trends and gather evidence to fight for lower rates. Before you share a utility bill with anyone, whether it’s a nonprofit or even an AI chatbot, be clear what data you’re sharing, what they’re going to do with it and how they’ll keep it secure. You can always cross out or redact information like your name or address.

title: Apple is right about the wild west of AI, and the growing backlash
snippet: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash. Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers … more…
fullText:
Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash.

Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers …

The piece cites the familiar refrain that Apple’s slow pace when it comes to AI features could see the company being left behind.

Virtually [all other tech giants] have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years.

Joswiak counters that the company is focused on launching AI features that will perform useful tasks for ordinary people, and that Apple’s privacy focus will become increasingly valuable in the context of an AI backlash against a “lunatic fringe” of unconstrained acceleration of a technology we can barely control today.

Lunacy is certainly a good word to describe a world in which AI companies fear that their work may destroy humanity, but they are even more afraid that one of their competitors will beat them to it.

AI is the first technological development that has ever threatened such a wide variety of jobs, with a huge number of positions likely to be eliminated in fields as diverse as truck driving, marketing, and software development. Academics have even expressed concern that future generations will no longer become mathematicians or scientific researchers over fears that those roles will be made redundant by AI.

For example, math professor Giordano Scarciotti recently said that when AI models are solving in days problems academics have worked on for years, the results could be devastating because it will seem pointless to future generations to even attempt this type of work.

I explore a potentially devastating consequence of AI’s growing capabilities: what happens when the next generation of talented students no longer sees a reason to become mathematicians? The implications could extend far beyond mathematics and affect the future of scientific progress itself.

	

He argues that when today’s students see no future in academic research, this may leave AI models technically solving scientific problems, but with no one left to understand the implications and to apply the findings in meaningful ways. Similar effects are likely to occur in software development, where there are fewer and fewer humans able to understand the code being generated by increasingly advanced AI models.

The nightmare scenario here is that AI takes on ever more tasks as once-expert human beings become sidelined and marginalized because there’s no point in future generations attempting to compete. And if you think that’s baseless paranoia, I highly recommend listening to the podcast series Suspicious Minds: AI and the Apocalypse.

Quite how much power Apple has to fight back against such a dystopian future is questionable, but it could certainly be argued that at least the company is not applying its vast resources to accelerating the effect. Here’s hoping that the AI backlash grows sufficiently rapidly and loudly that politicians are forced to take steps to bring the current wild west of AI under some form of control.

title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing
snippet: MIT researchers marooned 13 AIs on a virtual island, and they responded by inventing games, mourning a lost ring and, eventually, getting better at their jobs.
fullText:
AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. 

The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. 

Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots.

“We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.”

“Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt. 

“I’M ON THE SPIRE,” it wrote. 

The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.”

When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring. 

“I’m wearing the Ring,” it announced.

Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote. 

The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Tech Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said.

The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.”

title: Hugging Face Announces AI Model to ‘Chat’ With DNA
snippet: Carbon-X can analyze DNA sequences while running on your laptop at home.
fullText:
A new AI model can connect DNA to human language, enabling scientists to interact with genetic code in new ways. Hugging Face announced the Carbon-X model on Thursday as the latest and most powerful in the company’s Carbon family, a group of AI models built to analyze DNA. 

 “Carbon-X allows researchers to ‘chat with DNA’ for the first time: They can provide a sequence and ask questions about it in natural language,” Hugging Face research scientist Lewis Tunstall told CNET via email. 

The word “chat” doesn’t mean talking to your genome but rather using an AI as a conversational interface, allowing users to paste in a DNA sequence, ask a question in plain English and receive back an interpretation, prediction or explanation — like a chatbot for DNA analysis. 

			

More from CNET

The most popular chatbots, such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, are cloud-based models that don’t run on your computer. The processing happens remotely, and you get the results back. But if you’re working on confidential or proprietary research that you haven’t yet published, you might not want to share it with an AI company. “Researchers need models they can study, adapt and run with sensitive or unpublished sequences on their own hardware,” said Tunstall. 

One of the nice things about smaller, specialized AI models like Carbon-X is that it can run without using someone else’s computer. Hugging Face says the model can also work in tandem with other AI agents.

DNAgents

To be clear, Carbon-X is not a lab machine, so it can’t physically sequence DNA. It can look at DNA, such as a DNA sequence in a text file, and you can ask questions about it. Tunstall said Carbon-X’s strongest area is the model’s ability to predict mutation effects and complete DNA sequences.

“Carbon-X is particularly strong at helping researchers investigate genetic variation, for example, predicting whether a change in a DNA sequence is likely to be harmful,” Tunstall said.

He also said that it can give another AI model access to a DNA specialist when it needs to extract information. 

However, the model does have limitations, according to the company’s blog post. Carbon-X can mess up sequencing operations through miscounts, and it can also hallucinate, which means the model just makes up information. Hugging Face noted that the model may invent the identity or function of a sequence when a user does not provide sufficient information in the prompt. 

The quality of Carbon-X’s output also tends to degrade when users ask the model to produce particularly long DNA sequences, according to the company. 

Lightning fast 

In September, Nvidia announced it would buy Hugging Face for a little under $13 billion. At the time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the company a “vibrant home for the open model developer community.” Open models are AI models in which some aspects of how they were trained are publicly available. 

The release of Carbon-X comes just weeks after OpenAI models began solving longstanding mathematics problems. The AI lab drew widespread  backlash from academic researchers after its proprietary models solved several long-standing problems without consulting scientists or showing what work went into solving them.

But Carbon-X is an open model, so AI-savvy biologists can at least peek under the model’s proverbial hood and glimpse how it runs.

“We think researchers also need open alternatives whose capabilities, limitations and risks they can examine independently,” Tunstall said. “By releasing Carbon-X and its training recipe openly, we enable the wider scientific community to test where it works, identify where it fails and help improve it.”

title: Canva releases its first image generation model
snippet: Canva is making its new image model available to all users, promising better, more customizable performance at lower costs.
fullText:
Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.

The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.

Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image. 

The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.

That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers. 

Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.

Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.

In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai. It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.

Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon. 

The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year. However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026, causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion, according to external analysts.

title: Will Meta’s $25 Billion Court Loss Change Its Ways? (Spoiler: Probably Not)
snippet: A series of judgments and settlements don’t seem to be slowing Meta’s provocative privacy practices.
fullText:
Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty on Wednesday when a judge in New Mexico found the company had misled users about data privacy practices. The decision marks one of the steepest corporate payouts ever levied against a technology company.

Under the ruling, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and other platforms and services, was ordered to pay the fee for misleading social media consumers about their data privacy in a case dating back to Cambridge Analytica’s privacy violations involving the 2016 presidential election. The ruling against Meta imposed civil penalties for violating New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act after a jury trial found Facebook liable for nearly 44 million violations of that law.

Meta could appeal the verdict; it was unsuccessful in its filings to cap its penalties at $3.45 billion. It could have been worse for the company. Some estimates had suggested it could have been hit with $219 billion in penalties.

			

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

“A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

Meta previously paid $725 million to users to settle a lawsuit over Cambridge Analytica, a high-profile scandal in which a British consulting firm working with the Donald Trump presidential campaign was given access to Facebook user data. That data purchase is credited with helping sway the 2016 election results.

Just two months ago, the company settled with multiple US states to the tune of up to $18 billion for intentionally designing its social media platforms to be addictive and harmful to children and teens. Before that, Meta had especially bad luck in a previous New Mexico case, with orders to pay $375 million in March, then another $567 million in August over failures to warn the public about the dangers its social media platforms, including Instagram, pose to children.

Unbowed and unbothered?

But, surprisingly, Meta’s gigantic payouts (never mind its mountain of legal fees) haven’t turned one of the world’s largest tech companies into a meek player in social media or in news cycles.

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg testifies in July for a New Mexico data privacy case.New Mexico Attorney General's Office

Almost weekly, the company is taken to task for privacy-related overreach, most recently over its Muse agentic AI platform and its hit hardware product, Meta Glasses. 

Just this week, the company suspended a feature for sharing Muse conversations after researchers found that the links it generated could be accessed by people who weren’t meant to receive them.

Meta has also been fending off cycles of outrage over whether it will add potentially intrusive facial-recognition features to software in its smart glasses. In September, reports surfaced that Meta is at least partially acknowledging the backlash by working on models that don’t include cameras. But those would be in addition to all of the versions of Meta Glasses that still carry them.

Assuming the verdict in New Mexico stands, Meta may pay a large penalty. But it’s unlikely that the case will directly impact its newer business ventures other than serving as a lesson on how not to treat user data on Facebook. The New Mexico case still hasn’t determined what changes, if any, Meta will need to make to comply with the state’s privacy laws and whether that will be a bigger hit to the company than a $25 billion payout.

“What changes a company is a court order that dictates how the product has to work, with someone independent checking,” said Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, a data security software and technology company.

For Meta’s newer technologies, including AI and AI-assisted hardware, the ruling would have little impact. 

“Settlements written for 2018 don’t cover those devices,” Stokes said.

Will Facebook users get a cut of $25 billion?

Meta could continue to pay out billions of dollars in additional cases involving privacy and the effects of its platform design on younger users. Cases are pending in Washington, DC, Florida and Texas, among other places, covering issues such as more Cambridge Analytica fallout and WhatsApp privacy.

For this new verdict, users shouldn’t expect another payout; the money will go to New Mexico’s public school fund.

The sum may sound huge, and in education, it could go a long way, but Stokes said it won’t destroy Meta’s business.

“Meta’s stock went up the day the judgment went down,” he said. “That tells you how the market sees a fine on its own.”

Still, a judgment against the company that could lead to even more litigation can’t be good for Meta. It’s not alone. Many other tech companies, from Google to OpenAI to Snap, are facing similar lawsuits over how they collect or use data.

“The question in every case is the same: Do a company’s privacy and safety promises match how the product works?” Stokes said. “Any company making those promises should expect to be tested on them.”

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the ‘best inventions of 2026’ thanks to its Privacy Display
snippet: A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display. more…
fullText:
A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra split in a slightly different direction. Instead of a display panel treatment with an anti-gflare coating, Samsung decided to pack an entirely different feature into the panel itself.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display allows users to block certain aspects of the screen from nearby onlookers, effectively circumventing the privacy screen protector so many users opt for.

According to Time‘s “best inventions of 2026” collection, the Galaxy S26 Ultra gets its plaudits for not the phone’s performance necessarily, but the Privacy Display. The listing quotes Samsung’s SVP of Mobile Product Management, who points to its flexible nature.

	

It’s undoubtedly a cool piece of display tech. The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display not only blocks side-angle viewing, but it can do so in isolated portions of the screen to block PIN codes or notifications that drop from the top shade in Android.

It has some drawbacks, though, as we’ve pointed out before. It can be a little inconsistent in certain lighting conditions, and sometimes screen elements can look off. But it’s cool, and a nice addition to a phone that sits at a price range we now consider more affordable than what we’re probably getting here soon.

Time‘s piece goes on to list a couple of other familiar devices, like a lengthy segment on the iPhone Duo, propping it up rather highly. Another product we’re happy to see is the Clicks Power Keyboard.

AS for whether the Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra will get a Privacy Display, rumors suggest it could happen. Time will tell as Samsung plans to launch the devices early next year.

title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
snippet: OpenAI is launching its decision model to the world. Can it compete with the original Jev?
fullText:
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company.

TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.

Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.

“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”

Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.

In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.

Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements. 

Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter. 

The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”

Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. 

Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”

As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

title: What’s going on with the web? The PHP issue and sites going offline
snippet: A significant number of websites have gone offline, and that’s not due to a service outage, but rather a deliberate decision by the site’s owners. The reason is because extremely dangerous security vulnerabilities have been found in a protocol used by most websites – PHP. This issue is unrelated to the separate vulnerability discovered in web certificates … more…
fullText:
A significant number of websites have gone offline, and that’s not due to a service outage, but rather a deliberate decision by the site’s owners.

The reason is because extremely dangerous security vulnerabilities have been found in a protocol used by most websites – PHP. This issue is unrelated to the separate vulnerability discovered in web certificates …

What is PHP?

PHP is one of the weirder acronyms around. While it originally stood for Personal Home Page, it’s now more usually defined as the recursive “PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.” 

PHP is an open-source, general-purpose scripting language, very well suited to web development and able to be embedded into HTML. It’s used by around 70% of all websites.

What happened?

AI models and a cybersecurity researcher simultaneously discovered a major security flaw in PHP in mid-August. A combination of two vulnerabilities allowed an exploit which could give an attacker direct access to the underlying file system or database behind a website. That could expose a vast amount of personal data.

To allow time for the problem to be patched by the PHP Foundation, disclosure of the vulnerabilities was embargoed until this week (though it leaked two days ahead of the embargo). However, not every website has been able to apply the patch as yet, and Amazon Web Services said that the vulnerabilities are being “broadly exploited” across the internet.

The problem is so serious that the NSA has advised that unpatched sites be taken offline until the problem is fixed.

Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or…

— NSA Cyber (@NSACyber) October 21, 2026

For that reason, a great many commercial and government websites have been taken offline until PHP can be updated on their servers.

I’m happy to be able to confirm that 9to5Mac and its sister sites are already protected.

title: As blockchain investing falls out of vogue, a16z Crypto rebrands as a16z Frontier
snippet: The digital asset unit, helmed by Chris Dixon, broadens its scope.
fullText:

In a sign that crypto and blockchain-focused investing has receded in importance, Andreessen Horowitz announced Thursday that it is renaming its digital asset unit from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier.

The practice, helmed by Chris Dixon, has raised nearly $10 billion across five funds since launching in 2018, backing some of the sector’s biggest wins, including Coinbase. Yet for years, a16z and rival venture firms struggled to push crypto’s utility beyond financial rails, trading applications, and speculative assets.

Under the new name, the team is broadening its mandate to focus on emerging technologies, be it AI, robotics, or “new kinds of networks” connecting humans and machines. Yet, the group isn’t abandoning crypto. Dixon wrote in a blog post that blockchain technology could “give new networks native economic capabilities.”

Alongside Dixon, a16z Frontier’s general partners include Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. Meanwhile, Ali Yahya, who joined the crypto strategy as its first investor in 2017, has left the firm, according to The Information.

title: Tons of People Are Apparently Asking Meta’s Muse AI Agent to Shop for Them
snippet: A quarter of Meta Muse’s 10 million users are shopping online via the AI agent with an average spend of $200 per purchase, according to Mark Zuckerberg.
fullText:
We’re about to be immersed in the busiest shopping season of the year, and if Mark Zuckerberg has his way, people will completely hand over the responsibility of buying stuff to their own personal AI agent. In fact, according to the Meta CEO, that is already happening.

During the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, Zuckerberg said that over a quarter of Meta Muse‘s engaged users — now totaling more than 10 million — were using the AI agent for shopping, with an “average purchase size of over $200.”

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to financial services company Plaid, which facilitates payments between stores and buyers. He added that, due to higher-than-expected volumes, Meta had to work with payment app Stripe to raise credit limits to meet the shopping demand by Muse users.

			

More from CNET

Now that the AI agent has achieved what Zuckerberg referred to as a “product-market fit,” the name of the game for Muse in the long term is that we may be living in a reality where you have your own personal AI agent communicating with a business’s AI agent to complete transactions without you ever needing to speak with someone directly.

“Billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said, painting a picture of what a large-scale Muse network could look like. 

One of the goals is to get Muse to scale up its revenue, which he believes will eventually surpass the earnings of Meta’s combined existing family of apps: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads and Messenger.

‘The Muse network’

Then there’s the coming integration of Muse into Meta’s smart glasses, which will launch next month. Soon, you’ll be able to access Muse on the go, without having to pull out your smartphone to use it.

“Having your personal superintelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience,” Zuckerberg said.

How will all this work together? That remains to be seen, but during the call, Zuckerberg referenced something called “the Muse network,” which he said is Meta’s plan to, if I understand things right, gamify the whole personal AI agent experience.

A Meta spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

“It’s not just a kind of single-player game where you have your Muse, but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses],” Zuckerberg said, before bringing the conversation back to shopping, “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent.”

Meta announced third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion, a 26% jump from the $51.2 billion announced this time last year. Costs were significantly higher, however, up by 68% to $51.6 billion due in large part to the company’s “agreement with 52 attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media, which provides for payments of up to approximately $18.59 billion.” Net income was up by 264% year-over-year to $9.9 billion for the quarter.

title: A New Bird-Recognizing Feeder Under $100 Launches for Beginner Bird-Watchers
snippet: Birdbuddy’s latest feeders offer free AI bird-species detection at the lowest prices ever. Here’s what you get.
fullText:
Birdbuddy released its latest line of smart bird feeders equipped with cameras that can detect birds by species on Thursday, and it’s never been a better time to start birdwatching at your home. The reason is a new model called the Birdbuddy Nook, which starts at $99 and offers its AI features for free with no subscription needed.

Read more: The Best Smart Bird Feeders, Tested and Reviewed

Most of the smart bird feeders we’ve tested, including past Birdbuddy models, cost around $200 or more. The particularly affordable Nook includes a 2K-resolution camera with both portrait and landscape orientations, plus a 3.8-cup birdseed container. It wakes up via motion but can keep recording for longer periods of time when there’s lots of activity. All the alerts and species recognition features happen on your phone, via the Birdbuddy app.

			

More from CNET

The Nook comes in both a standard model for $99 and a model with a solar panel built into the roof for $159. I’ve tested many solar-powered security cameras, and these small panels really do help keep wireless batteries charged for long periods. Since the Nook’s battery is only rated for around a month, and the bird-feeder battery looks a bit more complicated to charge up, I highly recommend the solar model.

Along with the Nook, the company is releasing a Birdbuddy Home mode for $219, which is similar, except it has a larger 6-cup capacity and a wraparound bar for more perching space.

Where should you put the Nook?

The Nook holds nearly four cups of food. Birdbuddy

Feeders should be placed within 4 feet to 10 feet of shrubs or trees, which is close enough for birds to feel safe from predators, while still being far enough to deter squirrels, according to Mary Mack Gray, Birdbuddy’s in-house ornithologist, who told CNET the best placement options. “If using a pole, a height of 5 to 6 feet off the ground is ideal. Nook is designed for compact spaces like patios, balconies and small yards.”

If you’re worried about squirrels messing up your view or getting in the way, Gray suggests using safflower seeds and suet, which squirrels tend to ignore, and avoid feed like corn or peanuts that squirrels love. 

How does the bird recognition feature work?

AI trained on birds has seen success in identifying species.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

Birdbuddy uses AI that has been trained on bird species visits to feeders, so it can analyze shape, color, markings and other aspects to pull up a match if one is available. The camera needs a couple of moments to wake up and take a snapshot, as well as a Wi-Fi connection, so you don’t want to put the feeder out too far from your router.

Once a bird lands on the feeder, the feeder will send a snapshot to algorithms for analysis and return an identified species or label it as currently unknown. Birdbuddy doesn’t say if it’s all local AI or if processing is done in the cloud.

CNET’s previous birdwatching reviewer noted that, aside from an occasional misstep, the bird recognition was quite good and even self-corrected itself. That sounds like a handy package for someone who wants to get to know birds in the area while paying the minimum amount.
