title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony.ai and Nvidia
snippet: inDrive plans to begin testing Pony.ai's robotaxis in Kazakhstan's capital in the first half of 2027.
fullText:
Ride-hailing company inDrive, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.

The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.

Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.

Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.

The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London, where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner. Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.

inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.

“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”

Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.

“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.

The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.

The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.

Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.

Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.

“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”

Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.

“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”

inDrive operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries. The company has also expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.

title: Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display
snippet: The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for. more…
fullText:
The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for.

If you thought refresh rates couldn’t get any higher, it’s time to think again. Honor just announced four new devices, all of which push OLED refresh rates in impressive ways. The most impressive on the docket is probably the Honor Win Tablet, which packs an unbelievable 240Hz OLED display onto an actively cooled 8.4-inch tablet.

Honor looks to be pushing extreme processing speed with an included 15,000rpm fan build into the camera island on the back, which should keep the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 nice and cool. The display sports 6,000-nit peak brightness, 4,400Hz or 5,920Hz PWM dimming (refresh rate-dependent), a 10,000mAh battery with 66W charging, 12GB or 16GB RAM, 256GB or 512GB storage, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. The Win Tablet starts at CNY 4,499 (~$670).

The Honor Win2 is this year’s flagship gaming phone from the company, sporting two active cooling fans. One ramps up to 20,000rpm, while the side fan cranks that up to 31,000rpm, ensuring this thing should never, ever overheat despite the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 alleged overheating issues.

	

The Win2 sports a new top-of-the-line OLED panel with 10,000-nit peak brightness, a 185Hz refresh rate, 5,920Hz PWM dimming, 16GB RAM, 1TB of storage, a 200MP 1/1.4-inch main camera with OIS, 10,100mAh battery (not a typo!), 100W wired and 80W wireless charging, IP68/69/69K ratings, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. Holy cow what a flagship, and it starts at CNY 5,499 (~$990).

And if that’s not enough for you, there’s also the Honor Win2 RT, which dials the processor back just a tad to a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, keeps the active cooling fan, uses a physically smaller 200MP camera sensor, and even somehow increases the battery capacity to 12,070mAh. This one starts at CNY 4,199 (~$630).

Lastly, the Honor Win Turbo is the company’s mid-range offering for the line, packing a Snapdragon 8s Gen 4, drops the main camera to 50MP, and ditches the active cooling fan, but still retains the absurdly amazing 12,070mAh battery of the Win2 RT. The Win Turbo starts at CNY 3,299 (~$500).

Like the previous Honor Win series, this one appears to be largely relegated to China only. Honor confirmed to us that there won’t be a global release, but that doesn’t count specific regional releases out of the question.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price
snippet: Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak. more…
fullText:
Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak.

YTechB reports that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is headed to Europe with major price hikes in tow. Where last year’s Xiaomi 17 had a starting price of €999 with the Ultra at €1,499, the Xiaomi 18 Pro is starting the lineup at €1,449 this year. Xiaomi 18 Pro (256GB): €1,449

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (512GB): €1,849

The report goes on to cite the EU’s EPREL labels to confirm that global variants of the Xiaomi 18 Pro series will be cut down from the Chinese models. Xiaomi 18 Pro has a 7,000 mAh battery in China, but will only have a 6,000 mAh battery in Europe. Similarly, the Pro Max has an 8,500 mAh battery in China, but will be cut to 7,050 mAh in Europe. The base Pro is limited to 90W charging in the EU for reasons unclear.

	

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is among the first to adopt Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and launched in China last month. The timeline for a global release remains unclear at this point, but the MWC tech conference in Barcelona each Spring is often when Xiaomi kicks off availability. title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
snippet: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
fullText:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”

The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.

In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.

“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”

In publishing these results, Microsoft joins Google and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.

The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.

Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. 

Accuracy improvements delivered by DxO (no budget constraints) on CPC over models

prompted with baseline prompt across different large language models.Image Credits:Microsoft AI

Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.

With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost. 

DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.

Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.

Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare. 

“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”

Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.

“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.

He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.” 

“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”

Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.

“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.

He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’. 

Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time. 

“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”

Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes. 

“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs. 

Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts. 

“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

title: First Release Candidate for macOS 27.2 Golden Gate now available
snippet: Apple is rolling out the first RC for macOS 27.2 for developers and users enrolled in the public beta, ahead of the official release in the next few weeks. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple is rolling out the first RC for macOS 27.2 for developers and users enrolled in the public beta, ahead of the official release in the next few weeks. Here’s what to expect.

macOS 27.2 Golden Gate nears launch

After releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate beta 4 last week, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidate ahead of the system’s official launch in the coming weeks

macOS 27.2 adds support for five additional languages for Siri AI: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. The feature launched last month with English-only support, with Apple promising to expand language availability during its Surprise and Shine event.

One interesting under-the-hood addition in macOS 27.2 is new gesture recognition tools in several built-in apps, which could be laying the groundwork for Apple’s upcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro, expected to be announced later this month at the Pro and Tell event.

One particularly frustrating bug reported in beta 4 causes windows in Electron-based apps to randomly stop responding to dragging attempts. Restarting the Mac temporarily resolves the issue, but it can eventually return.

The build number for macOS 27.2 release candidate 1 is 26B118. We are digging through the system and will report back if we find any noteworthy tidbits.

Installing macOS 27.2 RC

Here’s how to install the first macOS 27.2 RC:

Back up your Mac

Open System Settings

Go to General ⇾ Software Update

Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates

From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta

Hit ‘Done’

title: I Went From AI Prompt to 3D-Printed Armor in 18 Hours
snippet: What started off as a dare became a fully fledged app in less than a day
fullText:
Tuesday morning, I received a notification from Google saying I could try out the new Gemini 4 Argon model. Normally, I just ignore it — I don’t really care which model it is, as long as it can help me with my day-to-day — but this time Google teased me with something close to my heart.

Gemini said it could “Create an app to model lampshades that I can 3D print.” My response, as CNET’s resident 3D printing expert, was, “I bet you can’t.”

Turns out, yes, it can.

			

More from CNET

I went from these first few screenshots to a fully 3D-printed object in under 18 hours, and I’m impressed by how easy it was.

Having a conversation with Gemini 4.0 is a lot like chatting with a designer or developer.Screenshot by James Bricknell/CNET

I’ll say upfront that I don’t really like generative AI. I think it uses people’s art and creative work without fair compensation, and I want to pay artists for their work. I changed the project from making lampshades to making cosplay armor and deliberately limited it to things I can already make myself. I know how to model greaves, pauldrons and vambraces, so this takes away nothing.

In my mind, this is analogous to a blacksmith who gets an apprentice to make the blanks for steel armor. The fine detail and character of the work is done by one person, but the grunt work is done by another. I can’t make very good chestplates or helmets, so I removed them from the app to focus on what I can make.

The planning stages

Talking to Gemini 4 feels the same as talking to any of the Gemini models. It understands what I’m saying and, more importantly, my intent. The first app Gemini created looked terrible on mobile. There were too many windows and not enough visuals of the model we were making. Explaining that the app was too messy and that we needed to clear it up got the response I wanted, rather than a bunch more questions.

The difference with Gemini 4 Argon is its ability to accomplish complex tasks at speed. Things like making complex web apps seem easy, and the time it took to give me new iterations was far less than with the Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite model I’m used to using.

I have Gemini Plus because I have a Google One plan, and I hit the token limit several times as I developed the app, but waiting an hour for a reset wasn’t that big a deal. If you have the Pro version, you’ll likely be OK.

The first few versions had too many options.Screenshot by James Bricknell/CNET

The first few versions of KeriForge (the name I settled on for my armor web app) were surprisingly usable right away. All the sliders for adjusting the model size worked. While they weren’t all intuitive, they had enough features to get me started. I kept going back, though. I removed some features, such as the helmet generator, and added new ones, including the strap hole marker and circumference calculator.

Gemini understood that these changes needed to reflect the physical nature of the end result. Instead of trying to cut holes in the digital model for the straps, it created marks on the model, so I could cut them out in the real world. 3D models need to be manifold — all their faces need to face the right way and connect to be “watertight” — otherwise, they can fail on the print bed. Making random holes in the model would most definitely cause it to fail.

Slowly getting the app dialed in.

At one point, I asked Gemini to let me “Download this onto my iPad Pro to make it easier to use.” Gemini understood that I didn’t want to make an iPad app, but that I wanted the web app to be available offline on my iPad. It made the app available as HTML and, once I got it up on Google Sites, told me how to download it using Safari.

It also has its own preview that lets me see the app running directly from the Gemini app on the iPad, so making changes was easy and instantaneous. It took around 10 iterations to reach KeriForge 8.2 and a state that I felt was good enough to produce a physical print.

The finishing touches?

Nomad Sculpt is powerful, and I ‘ve barely scratched the surface.

Creating the app was a lot of fun, and I learned a lot about how Gemini works and ways to prompt it to get a better finished article, but my original skepticism wasn’t that Gemini couldn’t make the app, but that it couldn’t produce a fully 3D-printable design that I could make physically.

I spent some time measuring my arm and adjusting the blank vambrace to make sure it would fit if it did print, then I hit the export button. Because I used my iPad, I got to export it directly to Nomad Sculpt, a 3D sculpting tool that let me add some random squiggles and an approximation of my name on the side of the model.

From there, I exported the file once again, this time to a browser app called Layerling. This app lets me edit the STL file — STL is the format for plain 3D models without any color — to cut the holes the straps need to go through. It’s a much more comprehensive program than the one I just made, so I know it can handle cutting the model while keeping it 3D-printable. I’ve only used Layerling a few times, but the more I do, the more impressive it becomes.

Making the holes in the model was simple, and since I had already asked Gemini to ensure there were guide markers, finding the right location was painless. Once I had cut those holes, it was onto the final stage: printing.

But will it actually print?

The defects were caused by the material, not the model Gemini produced.

Once I had the final STL ready for printing, it was a simple matter to export it over to Bambu Slicer and start the actual print. I chose to print it in TPU 75A, a flexible material I was already testing. TPU is a soft, rubbery material, so it can conform to my arm better than the more rigid plastics like PLA and ABS.

This was the moment when my bet with Gemini would come to fruition. After 7 hours of printing and about 11 hours of iterating and fiddling with Gemini, we would see whether the model actually worked or ended up as spaghetti all over my printer.

Printing it upright may not have been the right call.

The screenshot clearly shows that it did, indeed, work. You can see that, despite some errors that weren’t caused by the model, it produced a fully manifold and usable 3D print. The dimensions were perfect, fitting my forearm length and wrist circumference exactly.

The errors you can see on the model stem from the TPU being too soft and the model being too tall. As the printer increased the model’s height, the tension relaxed, causing the model to wobble under the print head. In the future, I would need to support it better in the slicer or print it lying down to achieve the print quality I expect.

An impressive AI tool

The final form of KeriForge works almost as I intend it.

I’m not an AI power user. I like to use Gemini to organize my emails, help me sort out spreadsheets, and that’s about it. I assumed that creating a web app capable of producing a fully physical product, such as a 3D model, would be arduous; that I would have to constantly refine my prompts to get it to understand my needs and wants. That wasn’t the case, though. Gemini Argon seemed to understand the context of what I wanted far better than I gave it credit for.

The term “prompt engineering” has always made me shy away from using these products. I don’t want to spend time trying to get an AI to understand what I need when a person could do it much more quickly. I can see now that by using that term, gatekeepers can put AI behind a knowledge wall: to present it as a mysterious, complex thing. It simply isn’t the case with the latest models.

I still don’t like generative AI, but I can’t help but be impressed by something that can take me from an idea to a physical product in less than a day. I went into this challenge betting Gemini 4 couldn’t do what it said it could, and was humbled in the process. I’m not going to start using AI for everything I do, but I’ve already thought of some fun ways it can help me with upcoming projects. Something that inspires my creativity can’t be all bad, can it?

Tuesday morning, I received a notification from Google saying I could try out the new Gemini 4 Argon model. Normally, I just ignore it — I don’t really care which model it is, as long as it can help me with my day-to-day — but this time Google teased me with something close to my heart.

Gemini said it could “Create an app to model lampshades that I can 3D print.” My response, as CNET’s resident 3D printing expert, was, “I bet you can’t.”

title: Arc browser gets a sunset date, and users have two months to move on
snippet: The Browser Company announced plans to discontinue its flagship Arc browser in favor of a new browser project called Dia. Today, Arc received a sunset date that gives users exactly two months to move on from the discontinued app. more…
fullText:
The Browser Company announced plans to discontinue its flagship Arc browser in favor of a new browser project called Dia. Today, Arc received a sunset date that gives users exactly two months to move on from the discontinued app.

Arc will be sunset on December 22

The Arc desktop browser is effectively what put The Browser Company on the map. However, the firm switched its focus to a second shot at taking on the desktop web browser with Dia. 

Since May of last year, we’ve known that Arc development was no longer moving forward. Now The Browser Company is giving users until December 22 to switch from Arc without losing information.

“We’ve decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026,” the company announced today. “That’s not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.”

The announcement goes on to explain why Dia is the solution moving forward.

“Our priority is to deliver best-in-class security for our members. Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI. Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”

Additionally, The Browser Company explains what users can expect when making the jump from Arc to Dia. It flags these four points:

Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.

Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.

Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.

The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Dia is available for free here. Separately, OpenAI shut down its AI-centric Atlas browser this year in favor of ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Several alternatives still exist on the Mac and beyond.

title: 1Password will let AI agents use your passwords without seeing them
snippet: As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control. more…
fullText:
As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control.

“1Password for Agents” is a new way to connect your password vault to your AI agents, all while leaving things secure. This works be connecting an AI agent like Meta’s Muse to 1Password and letting the agent ask for permission to sign into a website, at which point 1Password will provide the needed information on your approval. 

The actual sign-in is handled by 1Password, not the agent, with your credentials remaining hidden to the agent. 1Password explains:

1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password. The person sees which credential it needs and why, and then chooses whether to approve the request. If approved, 1Password fills it directly into the sign-in form. Once the website accepts the login, 1Password removes the credential so the agent can’t read or reuse it as it continues the task.

The process also leaves the rest of your password vault inaccessible to the agent.

	

While there’s still a level of trust, this solution seems far safer than just handing an AI agent your passwords. Right now this integration is limited to Muse and Grok Bot, but support for more agents is in the works, including OpenAI Dots and Anthropic Claude Duet.

title: New York and T-Mobile Settle Dispute Over 4G Plan Price Hikes. How to Get a Credit
snippet: Customers on T-Mobile One accounts from 2017 through 2019 could get a free 5G phone, credit toward a more expensive 5G phone or their last month’s payment and $25 gift card.
fullText:
T-Mobile has come to an agreement with the New York State Attorney General’s Office over claims that the carrier did not honor price guarantees for T-Mobile One plans on its 4G network between January 2017 and April 2019. Those plans were advertised as being “Price Guarantee Plans.”

Affected active T-Mobile customers who leave the carrier will be able to collect a credit worth the last month’s payment and a $25 gift card.

Those who stay on and are still using an older phone can get a free 5G phone (worth up to $250) or credit up to $150 toward a more expensive 5G phone for lines that are still using 3G or 4G. Rates for their recurring monthly plans will stay the same until 2029.

			

More from CNET

As part of the agreement, T-Mobile is also making a one-time payment to the Attorney General’s office in the amount of around $98,000.

According to a press release issued by New York Attorney General Letitia James, an investigation by the office found that T-Mobile raised rates on those plans in 2024 by approximately $5 per line, a change that affected approximately 252,957 plans at the time. It also pegs the relief to be worth around $38 million in value.

“T-Mobile misled hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers by promising that it would never raise prices on their cellphone plans, only to do exactly that just a few years later,” said James in the release. “Consumers shouldn’t have to pay the price for a misleading sale.”

The office’s filed agreement notes that T-Mobile made the price guarantee in at least two press releases and during a CNET video interview with then-CEO John Legere in 2017. In that video, Legere said, “We also extended the Un-contract to T-Mobile One Unlimited, which means we will never raise your rate; we guarantee.”

The agreement notes that T-Mobile ran afoul of a New York State law that requires companies to disclose terms “clearly and conspicuously,” and that any disclaimers about the price guarantee were ineffective by “directly contradict[ing] what a reasonable consumer would understand the Price Guarantee Offer to mean.”

It also states that “Respondent [T-Mobile] neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Findings” that detail the investigation’s conclusions.

When asked about the agreement, T-Mobile sent the following statement to CNET: “The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments. The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”

Per the agreement, T-Mobile has 150 days starting Oct. 20 to identify and notify customers who are eligible for the relief. After they’ve been notified, customers will have 45 days to decide whether to cancel their T-Mobile account (getting the last month’s payment and a $25 cash card) or continue as a customer (getting a free or discounted 5G-capable phone for each affected line or the $150 credit toward a new phone). For the latter, T-Mobile will also not charge any costs such as transfer or activation fees.

title: Google support pages start defaulting to AI chatbots – it might be for the best
snippet: Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page. more…
fullText:
Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page.

The Google Help portal is full of detailed articles that provide step-by-step processes for using a feature, documentation on where features are available or restrictions on them, as well as troubleshooting steps if something goes awry. It’s a massively useful resource, but one that Google is now changing.

Starting with support pages under Google Account Help, the company is shifting these support articles to an AI summary rather than a dedicated article. “Ask Google Help” will display a condensed version of the support article with direct troubleshooting steps, with the user then able to type in queries to have Gemini help figure out the next step forward.

A “View Sources” button at the bottom of the AI response allows users to still access the original article, but direct links to any of these articles now defaults to the AI experience.

	

An example can be seen below on the “Secure a hacked or compromised Google account” page that Google’s own support account directed users to within the past few days. It can also be seen on the “Fix common issues with 2-Step Verification” page and, as far as we can tell, any support pages on the Google Account Help forum.

Google, as of right now, appears to only be testing this on select support topics. The Google Pixel Help section, for instance, still defaults to articles, whereas the Google Chrome topic has also moved to the new experience.

Beyond support pages alone, this new design also impacts the central hub, with links to topics no longer showing by default in exchange for an AI chatbot that helps you find the relevant page.

Ironically enough, the Gemini topic is one of the ones missing this Gemini-powered experience.

9to5Google’s Take

While my initial reaction to this was skeptical, I think this is a rather good use of AI.

Google’s support page collection tends to be a bit of a labyrinth of links and vague search terms. Finding the specific page needed to address the problem you are running into can be very difficult. Meanwhile, Gemini’s inherent ability to understand natural language queries and find associated sources is very powerful in this regard.

I’m still a bit iffy on whether or not dedicated support articles should be converted into an AI summary (which Google still warns could be inaccurate), but using Gemini as a search and troubleshooting tool in this specific regard really highlights a strength of the technology.

What do you think?

title: Startup equips genetically enhanced dogs with Palmer Luckey’s military tech
snippet: The Warhound website calls this “a new breed of dominance.” | Image: Warhound A new Texas-based defense startup has a plan to improve military and police dogs in the US: it's going to genetically modify them and equip them with Anduril's military technology. fullText:
A new Texas-based defense startup has a plan to improve military and police dogs in the US: it’s going to genetically modify them and equip them with Anduril’s military technology. Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Ben Lamm, co-founder of Colossal Biosciences (the company that says it’s trying to resurrect extinct animals), and it’s already secured $200 million in funding from investors.

Warhound plans to use Colossal’s work in genetics, cloning, and animal biology to “produce healthier dogs with characteristics suited to demanding missions,” with Anduril then equipping them with its “advanced cybernetic Augments.” That includes eye and ear protection and EagleEye military technology to provide the dogs and their handlers with “greater awareness and protection in the field.”

“Man’s best friend deserves man’s best tech,” Luckey said in the press announcement. Bloomberg reports that despite having helped with the company’s conception, Luckey has no equity or ongoing role in Warhound.

The goal is to reduce dependency on Europe, where 80 percent of US military dogs are currently sourced, and improve the success rate of training the animals for specialist work. According to the startup’s press release, less than half of the dogs procured from overseas are typically deemed fit for service following the current three-year acquisition-and-training pipeline.

In a statement to TechCrunch, Lamm said Colossal is looking to enhance the animals by editing their genes to remove problems like poor eyesight and cancer likelihood, while adding new genes to improve performance “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot.” High-performance working dog breeds like the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd are the base of their studies, but the plan is to create “a new type of dog.”

These dogs don’t exist yet, but when (or if) they do, Warhound says they’ll be deployed for elite working roles in US military forces, emergency first response teams, and law enforcement. The American Humane Society will help to guide the company and certify its training programs. Marine veteran and intelligence specialist David Spirk has been named as Warhound’s CEO, and said the company’s goal is simple: “healthier dogs, better-prepared teams, and more service members and first responders coming home safely.”

title: Galaxy Watch user reports burn overnight; this isn’t the first time
snippet: One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation. more…
fullText:
One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation.

A post on Reddit shows blisters and red marks on a Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user’s arm (via Android Authority). Red marks and irritation aren’t all that uncommon for users, but they’re generally categorized as contact dermatitis. The blisters are new, though.

They claim the watch was on their wrist from the moment they went to bed after charging it to full, but that the battery had drained by the time they woke up. A dead battery might indicate the Galaxy Watch 5 Pro was active enough to burn through the 590mAh cell throughout the night. The user also notes their watch refused to power on after the incident.

When a lithium-ion battery depletes itself in a matter of hours, it puts off some considerable heat. So a burn this bad sits nowhere outside the realm of possibilities.

	

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen reports like this. Samsung’s Galaxy Watch lineup is, for the most part, consistently safe. We’ve tested them for years and have never had overheating issues that leave visible markings on skin. Still, reported battery issues are not all that uncommon. It’s even affected the Galaxy Ring.

Users have reported suspected overheating with their Galaxy Watch Ultra, Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 8, and a few other models in the past, but none of them seem to have affected the user as much as the most recent Watch 5 Pro report. An argument could be made for contact dermatitis on some older posts, but this report holds more water – or fluid.

What’s your experience with skin irritation from Samsung’s watches? Tell your story in the comments.

title: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear
snippet: Warhound, the brainchild of Ben Lamm and Palmer Luckey, emerges from stealth to genetically engineer dogs for military and law enforcement.
fullText:
Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. On Thursday, that idea came out of stealth as Warhound, backed by $200 million in funding from investors including Sequoia, 8VC, Corner Ventures, and In-Q-Tel, a venture firm backed by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.

Warhound’s dogs, which do not exist yet, will take on tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, such as bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the U.S. military’s working dogs come from Europe,  and less than half of them are fit for service.

That means the supply of working dogs is dwindling, and the U.S. increasingly relies on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the military and in law enforcement. Warhound aims to change that. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release.

Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where Luckey said more should be done for the military’s working dogs. The two kept in touch, and Lamm researched how working dogs are bred. He learned that many of them do not make it through training because of inherited predispositions to problems like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy. 

Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team studied top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking cell lines (living cells grown in a lab) from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, the team will edit the dogs’ genes, adding ones that will improve performance and removing ones that will not, to create “a new type of dog.” 

Anduril, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware, such as protection vests and goggles, to assist the dogs and their handlers with situational awareness and coordination. Lamm said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests with data sensors that send information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening. 

“The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions will make the dogs safer and healthier beyond their genetics, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes the enhancements will also better protect the dogs’ human handlers. 

Luckey is a partner in the venture but owns no equity in it, Lamm told TechCrunch. Colossal owns equity in the business and supports it by licensing its technology.

Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts to bring back animals like the dodo and the mammoth. As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and with identifying and copying animal genes. 

Lamm said the first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated, with births expected early next year and service ideally beginning within two years. Viagen, another Colossal-owned company, will partner with Warhound to clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s technology has a high cloning success rate, and Colossal already uses it in its program to protect endangered species.

Warhound doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs, but it expects to sell to first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. Asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business. 

Asked about civilian safety once genetically enhanced dogs enter service, Lamm said each dog will be trained like any military working dog and managed by whoever buys it.

The company said it is working under the guidance of the American Humane Society to help certify Warhound’s training program for the new dogs. The hope is also that when these new military dogs retire, they will enter the Society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program, which provides homes for retired military dogs — or another program the Society offers to help dogs.

This piece was updated to add Corner Ventures as an investor.

title: Retro gaming is being overrun with AI
snippet: Retro video games are everywhere lately - especially in places where they aren't supposed to be. Halo in a web browser, Wind Waker on the iPhone, Super Smash Bros. in mixed reality. Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it's also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games. Decomps and recomps - shorthand for decompile and recompile - are a form of reverse engineering that involves breaking a game down to … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Retro video games are everywhere lately — especially in places where they aren’t supposed to be. Halo in a web browser, Wind Waker on the iPhone, Super Smash Bros. in mixed reality. Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it’s also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games.

Decomps and recomps — shorthand for decompile and recompile — are a form of reverse engineering that involves breaking a game down to its building blocks and then rebuilding it so it can run on hardware it was never intended for. When done manually, it’s a slow, painstaking process. A group spent years decompiling the original Animal Crossing on the GameCube, for instance. But AI coding tools have cut that timeline down significantly, and the sheer number of ports has grown dramatically in recent months.

This summer, Chris Sotraidis, an AI consultant who works on game ports as a hobby, saw a port of Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour — which EA made open source last year — for the iPhone and iPad. The “technical challenges” inspired him to try making a handful of similar ports, including a mobile port of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using an existing community-built decomp of the game. Within just a few weeks, he was working on a dozen projects. He says that kind of productivity wouldn’t happen without the use of AI.

Some of those ports “would have been possible with minimal AI assistance if I’d had significantly more time,” Sotraidis says. “But I’m honest enough to say that the pace and volume would not have been possible for me without it. It would have been extremely slow by comparison. The tools allow you to move much faster if you know what you want.”

That speed has drawn many people to try out these AI tools, either for fun, the technical challenge, or for preervation reasons. It’s also a reason why there’s been what seems like a deluge of new projects popping up on platforms like Reddit, X, and GitHub. But these ports can be problematic from a preservationist perspective. One of the reasons why decomp projects exist in the first place is that users can pull a game apart and understand how it works, but that kind of understanding and knowledge is lost when AI does the work. Sure, you can put Spider-Man in a Batman game, but you probably won’t discover how certain programming decisions came to be, which can hurt the ability to restore games faithfully.

“The tools allow you to move much faster if you know what you want.”

The rapid pace of AI-driven decomps has overwhelmed the DIY scene. Last week, a community-focused website that tracks decomp projects and provides various resources abruptly shut down due to AI’s impact. “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way,” the site’s owner, writing under the pseudonym Encounter, said when announcing the shutdown. “What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways.”

Those ways include taking existing decompilation projects and “finishing” them with AI, as well as racing to quickly port decomps that the user never actually contributed to in the first place. In essence, one of the big problems is people who are using AI to rush through the process while building on the work of others. This is especially an issue given the community-centric nature of the existing decomp scene. “The bottom line is that these kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric,” Encounter wrote.

Given the ongoing challenges with video game preservation, in which it’s estimated that more than 90 percent of classic games are “critically endangered,” the rise of AI in the decomp scene can be seen as something of a double-edged sword. On the one hand, it has created a surge of interest, turning words like decomp and recomp from niche terminology to headline material, while allowing non-programmers the opportunity to experiment and test ideas. On the other hand, the speed and lack of attention to detail in many of these projects run counter to the aims of most preservationists, who try to not only keep games alive for modern audiences but also understand the way they were built. AI is a quick fix that could have long-term drawbacks.

This has created a divide, with those on the preservation side feeling disillusioned by the prevalence of slop, and those on the AI side excited by the possibilities, particularly as the tools continue to evolve. As Sotraidis explains, “I think a lot of what gets dismissed as slop today can improve as the tools get better and people learn to use them well. That doesn’t make the current criticisms invalid. Better tools aren’t automatically going to make people give proper credit or treat each other well. But I do think thoughtful creators and builders will be able to make even more amazing things, faster.”

For those vehemently against the use of AI in ports and decomps of classic games, they might be fighting a losing battle. AI tools seem to be infiltrating every aspect of game development, not just in the realm of hobbyist retro fans. Fortnite developer Epic Games recently launched a vibe-coded version of its PC games store, and it has reportedly shifted to “AI-accelerated development” for an upcoming collaboration with Disney. On X, Epic’s CEO Tim Sweeney wrote that he believes AI tools will lead to “a new golden age of gaming.”

Meanwhile, at least one major name has embraced the decomp scene. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma set up an internal division called Xbox Labs to explore the space and “turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” She noted, “While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life, and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators.” (Currently, the only thing the division has teased is an experimental dashboard.)

Xbox embracing decomps is particularly notable at a time when old games are serious business. Some of the biggest releases this year are remakes of Halo: Combat Evolved and Ocarina of Time, while Resident Evil has been rejuvenated in part due to a stream of strong remakes. The question for the future is whether audiences would rather play a lavish remake of Halo or a vibe-coded port that they can take anywhere.

excerpt:
Retro video games are everywhere lately — especially in places where they aren’t supposed to be. Halo in a web browser, Wind Waker on the iPhone, Super Smash Bros. in mixed reality. Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it’s also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games.

Decomps and recomps — shorthand for decompile and recompile — are a form of reverse engineering that involves breaking a game down to its building blocks and then rebuilding it so it can run on hardware it was never intended for. When done manually, it’s a slow, painstaking process. A group spent years decompiling the original Animal Crossing on the GameCube, for instance. But AI coding tools have cut that timeline down significantly, and the sheer number of ports has grown dramatically in recent months.

The photos that aren't the first one can be edited with softw … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Jay Peters

 

is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Etsy is announcing stricter rules about how AI can be used in listings to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform. In a post, the company says that “many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content” and that sellers are “concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways,” spurring the new policies and restrictions.

Under the new policies, every listing must include “at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background,” and all photos must “accurately represent the item a buyer will receive.” The photos that aren’t the first one can be edited with software or AI-powered tools, as long as “the final result remains an accurate representation of the physical product.” The company shared a few examples to demonstrate the type of misleading images that are prohibited, including the cat stuffed animal at the top of this post.

Image: Etsy

While uploading images for a listing, if Etsy detects that any may be AI-generated, the platform will show a pop-up where you can note if an image was made with AI or not, as shown in a video. If a buyer reports that what they receive is “materially different” from a listing, a seller may be responsible for a refund.

For sellers who offer “functional guides,” which include patterns, recipes, or instructions,” Etsy says that the information in those products “must be your own work, not generated by AI.” Sellers will have to show an “actual result” made from a guide. The company also says that listings made by bots are no longer allowed.

Selling AI-generated art is still allowed on the platform, but a seller must disclose that it was made with AI, Etsy says.

title: Apple wins again in copyright infringement battle over Apple TV thriller series
snippet: The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit today upheld a verdict from early last year that cleared Apple of allegations that one of its hit thriller series was copied from an independent film. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit today upheld a verdict from early last year that cleared Apple of allegations that one of its hit thriller series was copied from an independent film. Here are the details.

‘Servant’ cleared of copyright infringement allegations

When Apple announced its streaming platform, then known as Apple TV+, one of the many original productions it had in the works was M. Night Shyamalan’s psychological thriller Servant.

Starring Lauren Ambrose (Six Feet Under), Toby Kebbell (RocknRolla), Nell Tiger Free (The First Omen), and Rupert Grint (Snatch), the series “follows a Philadelphia couple in mourning after an unspeakable tragedy creates a rift in their marriage and opens the door for a mysterious force to enter their home,” per Apple TV’s synopsis.

Shortly after Servant premiered, however, Italian-born director Francesca Gregorini sued Apple and Shyamalan, alleging that the show stole the plot from her 2013 film “The Truth About Emanuel.” She sought as much as $81 million in damages.

While Servant ran for four seasons, wrapping up in 2023, the lawsuit dragged on until January last year, when a jury unanimously ruled in favor of Apple and Shyamalan. Jurors found that the show’s creators had not had access to Gregorini’s film before developing the series.

Gregorini subsequently appealed the verdict, challenging two aspects of the trial.

First, she argued that the jury should have received more detailed instructions on what constitutes “widespread dissemination,” including whether her film was sufficiently well known within the entertainment industry for the creators of Servant to have potentially encountered it.

She also challenged the trial judge’s decision to accept the verdict without first answering a question from jurors seeking clarification on the term “widespread dissemination.”

Today, as reported by Reuters, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected both arguments and upheld the jury’s verdict in Apple’s favor.

In its decision, the appeals court found that the jury instructions accurately reflected the applicable law and that the trial judge was not required to provide a more detailed definition of what it means for a work to be “widely disseminated.”

It also ruled that the judge did not abuse her discretion by accepting the jury’s unanimous verdict without first answering the jurors’ question.

title: Sensor Tower: Meta’s Muse app tops 10 million US downloads in 40 days
snippet: According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Sensor Tower reported that Meta’s Muse app had surpassed 5 million downloads in the US, thanks to a mix of popularity and Meta’s massive ad push.

At the time, the app had spent 12 consecutive days at the top of the US App Store. Muse has since slipped to second place, but Sensor Tower now reports that it has become just the 12th app to reach 10 million US downloads within 40 days of launch, since the firm began tracking apps in October 2015.

For comparison, Sensor Tower says ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude reached just 3.7 million, 500,000, and 200,000 US downloads, respectively, during their first 40 days.

Per Sensor Tower data, ChatGPT scaled to ~15mn global downloads in its first 40 days post app-launch, as its global reach expedited its growth. ChatGPT’s top regions by downloads during the studied period included the US, Japan, Brazil, and Germany, which accounted for 25%, 9%, 6%, and 5% of the global downloads, respectively.

The report also noted that ChatGPT’s US downloads have declined 25% over the past 30 days compared to the previous 30-day period. ChatGPT is currently the fourth most downloaded free app on the US App Store, while Claude ranks seventh and Grok 34th.

As for the other apps that reached the 10 million milestone within 40 days, Sensor Tower didn’t name them all, but noted that nine were mobile games. The most recent app to achieve the feat was Meta’s own Threads, back in July 2023.

	

Today’s report comes amid fresh privacy concerns surrounding Muse, after security researchers discovered that shared conversations could expose sensitive personal and business information. Meta has since suspended the sharing feature while it investigates the issue.

Despite the privacy concerns, Sensor Tower’s data suggests that Muse is doing a better job of retaining users than its AI competitors, which is not surprising, since this is one of Meta’s strongest suits:

US Muse users are returning to the app, which is averaging a 30% retention rate after 7 days, and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. Meta is currently outpacing AI competitors in its retention at the 7 and 14 day mark, as ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok averaged a 19% and 16% retention rate, respectively.

Finally, Sensor Tower notes that Meta continues spending heavily to promote its AI assistant. According to the report, the app accounted for 39% of Meta’s advertising spend in the US so far this month, up from 23% in September. Muse also reportedly climbed from 73rd to 21st place among US brands ranked by advertising impressions.

fullText:

OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC.

title: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max was exciting until I found out about the price
snippet: RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. You’re not reading that wrong. This non-foldable, MediaTek-powered Android flagship costs just a little bit less than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (€1,999). 

It’s not really Oppo’s fault, and it’s not like the company is alone in this struggle. A comparable Galaxy S26 Ultra in Europe isn’t much cheaper at €1,769, and Xiaomi is also rumored to be running into wildly high prices for its next launch in Europe too. This is just the current state of the tech industry as a whole, largely thanks to AI companies. 

But the reactions to Oppo’s pricing have not been quiet, and not just for the European model. Some users on Reddit mention how Oppo’s price matches the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max, how pricing in some regions is disproportionately high, and how you can still get the Find X9 Ultra for less. And I’m right there in that same train of thought.

	

As mentioned in our review, you’ll be happy with the Find X10 Pro Max. It performs well, has great cameras, and killer battery life, but this price tag really stings in a market where prices are already exceptionally high. 

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Even the Find X9 Pro seems like a better deal for many – some have pointed out that last year’s flagship has more memory and a bigger battery in Europe for hundreds less. You can get a Find X9 Pro in Europe right now for around €1,000~, way less than the newer model.

Find X9 Pro and Ultra both deliver more phone for less money

You might be able to get the Find X10 Pro Max for a deal, though. Some UK buyers point out offers they were able to take advantage of, but nothing changes that Oppo’s latest flagship is very expensive.

title: iOS 27 adds scam-prevention feature to iPhone, here’s how to enable it
snippet: iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it.

Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can detect suspicious activity in real time to prevent scams

Every day around the world, people get tricked into sharing sensitive information like bank details or other financial info with bad actors.

This commonly happens via text messages, emails, or phone calls to iPhone or Android devices. And while iOS has built-in tools like call and message screening, those tools can’t prevent a scam if you choose to take action on it.

But iOS 27 introduces a new level of scam-prevention with a security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection.’

Here’s what it does, per Apple’s website:

Impersonation Risk Detection helps protect against active social engineering scams. In these scams, an attacker might pose as a bank, government agency, or someone you trust to pressure or guide you into making a payment or changing your account details. Traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t always detect this kind of scam. That’s because you’re taking the action, even though you’ve been tricked or pressured.

Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes information about your device and Apple Account to help detect signs of an active scam. Based on this analysis, it returns a risk level to the app. The app receives only the risk level, not the underlying information used to generate it. The app decides what to do next. For example, it might ask you to verify your identity, add a delay, or show a warning.

You can turn Impersonation Risk Detection on in iOS 27 by going to Settings ⇾ Privacy & Security ⇾ Impersonation Risk Detection then toggling on ‘Share with App Developers.’

Impersonation Risk Detection is only available in supported apps, and Apple hasn’t published a list of those apps at the moment. But once enabled, it provides the app with a “risk level” while omitting the underlying information driving it. Risk levels include:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected

Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected

High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected

Once the app has this risk level, it decides what action to take. For example, it may prompt you to offer additional authentication, or show a warning message related to scams.

For more details on how the feature works using ‘Trust Insights,’ see our coverage here.

fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Brick, the company behind the $59 gadget that blocks you from using apps on your phone, has launched a new device that’s designed to help you cut back on doomscrolling in bed. The $129 Brick Night introduces a location-based element: instead of requiring you to tap your phone against the device, like the OG Brick, this version uses Bluetooth to automatically kick in when you enter your bedroom (or any other room you put it in).

The Brick Night uses two CR2477 batteries, and you can set a location zone of up to 25 feet x 25 feet. Both this and the Brick allow you to select specific apps to block instead of rendering your entire phone inaccessible, but the pitch with the Night version is that the blocking happens automatically in the background when you enter the room, and so won’t interrupt or add new steps to your usual bedtime routine.

Brick’s night version also supports multiple users, and each can independently configure their own settings, modes, blocked app selection, time windows, and spaces. Still, the Brick Night is more than twice the price, and because it doesn’t include NFC capabilities, it can’t be used for both location-based and tap-based blocking — which would allow it to replace the original Brick.

title: Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer
snippet: Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection. more…
fullText:
Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection.

Chrome is adding suspicious site warnings in the address bar “when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites.” There are two tiers:

Suspicious sites (lower confidence verdict, possible risk of user harm)

Dangerous sites (high confidence verdict, high risk of user harm)

Suspicious sites (above) will trigger a shield icon in the Omnibox, with a dialog box letting you “Mark as safe” or go “Back to safety.” 

Dangerous site alerts (below) will continue to appear as a “full-page red interstitial warning.”

	

Meanwhile, Chrome is continuing to boost scam detection by leveraging Gemini models in the cloud after using on-device approaches. This protects Enhanced Protection users from a broader range of threats, including fake antivirus and browser update scams.

This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites.

Safe Browsing uses the Gemini analysis “in combination with domain reputation and other security signals.” Google will process page content ephemerally, “meaning it is never logged, retained, or used to train models.”

The final Enhanced Protection update defends against ClickFix social engineering that “tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands on their own computers in order to ‘fix’ a fake issue.” In reality, this is used to “carry out malicious actions such as downloading and setting up malware.”

Because these utilities are native to the system and trusted by security software, bad actors use them to blend in and hide their activity, and by shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.

When a potential ClickFix script is copied, Chrome will remove personally identifiable information from the clipboard and send it to Safe Browsing for further analysis. The browser shows a warning if a “dangerous verdict is returned.”

This system is designed to be high precision, in order to protect users in real time while minimizing disruption to legitimate developer activity.

Enhanced Protection was introduced in 2020, and Google said it was enabled by 1 billion users in 2025. It can be enabled in Chrome Settings > Privacy and security > Security.

title: Constrained iPhone Duo availability is annoying, but a mixed blessing for Apple
snippet: Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year. That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … more…
fullText:
Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year.

That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … 

Apple always builds up inventory before launching new products, but with new product categories like the first foldable iPhone it can be hard for the company to predict demand. 

In many ways, the company is in a no-win position with this balancing act of supply and demand. If demand greatly exceeds supply, Apple risks irritating some of its most loyal customers – those who are willing to go all in on a first-generation product. But if supply exceeds demand, and a new product remains available for immediate delivery, commenters will inevitably point to that as evidence for it being a flop.

The balance of supply and demand

In truth, none of us knows the true position here. The imbalance may be due to the iPhone Duo being wildly more popular than Apple anticipated (as the company implies), or it may be that demand is modest but manufacturing complexities mean that supply is even more limited. My own view is that it’s likely a mixture of the two: relatively high demand and rather constrained supply.

Relatively high demand because, while foldables in general are still a rather niche product, it’s very clear that Apple put in a lot of thought and work into making this one the best on the market. The company has seemingly addressed the two main issues that beset Android foldables to date: a visible crease and poor durability. The company then created software features to take full advantage of the form factor of the device, and topped it off with an absolutely superb launch video. I think some of those who had previously ruled it out on the basis of price changed their minds once they saw it; It’s been a long time since we’ve seen such excitement levels around a new Apple product.

Rather constrained supply because it’s clear that the complexity of the device, and most especially the hinge, means that it’s very difficult to manufacture, and it’s likely that yield rates are relatively low.

A mixed blessing

One of the biggest problems of the world we live in today is polarization of views. Large swathes of the population seem to have lost sight of the fact that two different things can be true at the same time.

	

Yes, pre-ordering a product in October within minutes and then having to wait until January to receive it is both annoying and frustrating. If I were in that position, I would absolutely be pissed at Apple.

But also yes: this immediate slipping of delivery dates adds to the narrative of a wildly popular new product, serving to further boost the hype around it. 

If Apple could have perfectly predicted demand, then it would likely have wanted a position where delivery times slipped sufficiently for the launch to be viewed as a success, but not so much that customers get annoyed. This situation isn’t ideal, for sure, but in my view it’s more of a mixed blessing than a strategic error.

Finally, if you are the position of having been given a lengthy wait for your order, the reality may not be quite as bad as it appears. Apple tends to present customers with the worst case dates initially, often bringing them forward subsequently. Additionally, retail staff tell me that there will often be unexpected walk-in stock available at some stores, again due to imperfect forecasting of online versus offline sales, as well as varying demand at different stores. That’s always worth trying from the day after the new devices go on sale.

title: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
snippet: Microsoft points the blame for ConnectWise's breach at a China-aligned hacker, which relied on AI agents to rapidly hack into thousands of its customers.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

9:47 AM PDT · October 22, 2026

Image Credits:Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

The bad week for cybersecurity just got worse for thousands more companies, who were spied on by Chinese hackers following the breach of IT management and remote access giant ConnectWise.

Security researchers at Microsoft say the China state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials that are used to establish data links between ConnectWise and its corporate customers, who rely on the cloud service to back up their company’s data. 

By stealing the credentials, the hackers could log in to the customer’s Microsoft-hosted environment as if they were an authorized user and access their emails and other files.

According to Microsoft, the hackers used AI agents to rapidly hack into around 2,250 organizations at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders “little time to detect and respond.”

The speed of the mass-hacks was attributed to the use of AI agents, specifically ARTEX, an open source AI framework that works with AI models to stress-test cyber defenses. The same AI software was used in a recent compromise of South Korea’s financial systems, many of which had weak security and lacked multi-factor authentication.

ConnectWise said it’s paused access to its cloud backup system and is investigating the breach. As of Thursday, the company said it was working on restoring the service.
