title: iOS 27.2: Three new features coming to your iPhone next week
snippet: iOS 27.2 is about to launch, arriving as the next big iPhone update—iOS 27.1 is iPhone Duo-only. Here are three new features coming next week with iOS 27.2. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is about to launch, arriving as the next big iPhone update—iOS 27.1 is iPhone Duo-only. Here are three new features coming next week with iOS 27.2.

#1: Dual Capture for Group FaceTime

FaceTime got one of its biggest upgrades in years with iOS 27. 

On compatible iPhone models, Dual Capture lets you display both your front and rear camera views at the same time. Just tap the ‘Flip’ button and the back camera will go live while the front camera remains active.

And in iOS 27.2, the feature gets even better by adding support for Group FaceTime calls.

iOS 27 only lets you use Dual Capture in one-on-one calls, but with iOS 27.2 it’s available for Group FaceTime too.

#2: Apple Podcasts overhauls ‘Up Next’ queue

Apple Podcasts gets a key change in iOS 27.2 that I’m a big fan of.

The previous ‘Up Next’ queue at the top of the app’s Home tab is now split into two new sections:

New Episodes replaces Up Next, and contains the latest releases for shows you follow

Continue Playing is brand new, located directly below New Episodes as a hub for all in-progress shows

I’ve criticized the Up Next feature before for being cluttered and confusing, so I’m very excited to see this change. After testing it during the beta, I think it’s a huge improvement that helps users better keep track of everything they’re listening to.

#3: Apple TV app supports user profiles

Apple’s TV app is about to support user profiles on iPhone, bringing the feature over from tvOS to iOS for the first time.

When you first launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll see a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it from ever showing up again. But if your child ever watches videos on your iPhone, you might be very glad about this new feature.

With profiles, the Apple TV app can change which content it displays and recommends based on the selected viewer. And importantly, when a child’s profile is active, they’ll only see age-appropriate series and movies from Apple. So not only does your own personal viewing queue stay uncluttered, but you also ensure your child doesn’t see something they shouldn’t.

title: Netflix can’t fire its way out of this downward spiral
snippet: Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters assured investors this week that they have nothing to be concerned about. Sure, the company was going to lay off 1,000 employees, downsizing its product, tech, and legal departments, and was ousting its chief content officer, film chairman, and film vice president. But it had also hired a new COO - "one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry," Sarandos said - to turn things around. Though executive shake-ups aren't uncommon, having so many of them back to back would send a concerning message even in the best of circumstances. With Netflix, however, the situation lo … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters assured investors this week that they have nothing to be concerned about. Sure, the company was going to lay off 1,000 employees, downsizing its product, tech, and legal departments, and was ousting its chief content officer, film chairman, and film vice president. But it had also hired a new COO — “one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry,” Sarandos said — to turn things around.

Though executive shake-ups aren’t uncommon, having so many of them back to back would send a concerning message even in the best of circumstances. With Netflix, however, the situation looks undeniably grim given the streamer’s recent troubles with missed ad revenue targets, sluggish growth, and a failed attempt at acquiring Warner Bros. Losing WB to David Ellison’s Paramount was a huge blow — that merger would have given Netflix an easy way to expand its catalog, grow its user base, and build a more established presence in movie theaters. The company now has to navigate those challenges on its own while also figuring out why its current content slate hasn’t resulted in record profits.

Sarandos admitted that Netflix needs “better execution” in the US

While Netflix has put out some well-received fare like East of Eden, Adolescence, and The Diplomat, the company is well known for canceling series before they’ve even had a chance to build an audience. People frequently complain that they rarely see advertisements for Netflix’s new projects, but when they do, it tends to be for weird misfires like The New Stanford Prison Experiment and Wonka’s The Golden Ticket. In each of the recent executive firings, you can see Netflix trying to signal to investors and the public that it has a clear understanding of what hasn’t been working with its output from the past few years. There’s no denying that Netflix’s recent lineup has been lackluster, but these issues feel like they’re endemic to the company itself rather than something that can be blamed solely on a trio of executives.

Sarandos insisted to investors that Netflix’s “content around the world is largely working,” but he admitted that the company needs “better execution” in the US, where business is “just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”

Netflix’s push into more markets around the globe was largely led by Bela Bajaria, who led TV and content at Netflix over the past decade. Bajaria ushered the streamer into a new era of being a hub for unscripted programming, sports, and internationally produced projects. Bajaria is part of the reason that a Netflix subscription gives you access to WWE and Lupin as well as Bridgerton.

On paper, Bajaria did exactly what she was hired to do. She expanded and diversified Netflix’s library of content, hoping to attract more people to the platform. Bajaria was instrumental in the production and rollout of international series like Money Heist and Squid Game — the latter of which became a global phenomenon and boosted subscriptions while also winning the streamer a few Emmys. Netflix’s current approach to acquiring and distributing international programming has been so successful that Sarandos said the company has no plans to change its strategy. But it seems that success was not enough to protect Bajaria’s job.

In a statement about incoming COO Peter Rice’s hiring and Bajaria’s dismissal, Sarandos thanked her for her “dedication, innovation, creativity and leadership” and said he was grateful for “everything she’s done to help Netflix entertain the world.” But that gratefulness didn’t exactly gel with recent reports that Bajaria is being used as a scapegoat and was axed with little notice.

Film chairman Dan Lin — who joined Netflix in 2024 and reported directly to Bajaria — exited Netflix in a somewhat similar fashion to his former boss. After years of courting filmmakers with massive production deals, Netflix hired Lin to help it rein in its spending. Lin had a strong track record of producing financial hits for other studios, like Warner Bros.’ The Lego Movie and Disney’s live-action Aladdin. Lin also appointed Doug Belgrad as VP and tasked him with overseeing Netflix’s lineup of original content. By all accounts, Lin did exactly what Netflix courted him for, and his mind for austerity was aligned with the company’s larger goals. But as The Hollywood Reporter notes, Lin’s brusque personality could sometimes lead to friction with some of the high-profile talent Netflix is in business with, like Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew auteur Greta Gerwig and AI startup InterPositive founder Ben Affleck.

Price hikes have undoubtedly soured some people on the platform

While much of Netflix’s recent programming is the product of Bajaria, Lin, and Belgrad’s leadership, they were not the only people responsible for turning the streamer into what it is today. In recent years, Netflix has also gotten into podcasts and gaming — initiatives that have often felt like desperate attempts at clawing back attention from rivals like YouTube, TikTok, and any one of the free ad-supported television platforms on the market. The fact that there are so many other different services that Netflix’s subscribers might prefer to spend more time on is one of the biggest challenges. And many of these competitors have become more attractive to customers as Netflix has continuously raised its prices.

Aside from introducing ad-supported tiers, forcing subscribers to pay more has been Netflix’s primary method for revenue growth. Netflix isn’t unique in that regard — all of the major streamers are doing it — but it has undoubtedly soured some people on the platform at a time when its offerings haven’t always felt like they justified their price. Even when Netflix has stumbled its way onto unexpected gems like KPop Demon Hunters, the company doesn’t always seem to have the strongest game plan to capitalize on their success. Rice’s hiring does suggest that Netflix knows it has to do things differently, and his past may provide some insight into the streamer’s future plans.

Before coming to Netflix, Rice served as 21st Century Fox’s president until the studio was acquired by Disney. Rice became Walt Disney Television’s chairman in 2019 and oversaw production for a number of the company’s networks, including ABC and FX. And after being fired by Bob Chapek in 2022, Rice pivoted into producing projects like Jason Reitman’s Saturday Night, 28 Years Later, and the upcoming Elden Ring movie. Rice’s roots in traditional studio film development points to Netflix getting even more serious about screening its films in theaters. The streamer already has plans to give The Magician’s Nephew and the KPop Demon Hunters sequel sizable theatrical runs, and it is currently trying to secure Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s La bola negra an Academy Award at the upcoming Oscars.

Having a larger presence in movie theaters won’t solve all of Netflix’s problems, but it could help shift the way that people perceive the platform and its catalog. And in Sarandos’ assertion that Rice has a deep understanding of talent relationships, you can hear that the co-CEO is banking on his new COO to convince filmmakers that Netflix is where they need to bring their latest ideas. Rice’s hiring makes for a compelling narrative about Netflix finding its way forward by relying on the instincts of an industry veteran known for effortlessly jumping between the film and TV worlds. But that narrative doesn’t feel quite as convincing when you look back at the way Netflix’s partnerships with directors like David Fincher, Shawn Levy, and Noah Baumbach resulted in some pretty terrible projects.

In order for Netflix to really turn the ship around, it has to realize that content is only one piece of the puzzle. Splashy new movies and series won’t mean much if people don’t feel that the service is financially accessible, but Netflix’s vague allusions to “improving” monetization suggest that the service is only going to get more expensive. Right now, Netflix needs to be focused on demonstrating that it has a clear plan for how it can move into the future. The company can start by acknowledging the larger issues with its business model instead of simply throwing executives under the bus.

With Netflix, however, the situation looks undeniably grim given the streamer’s recent troubles with missed ad revenue targets, sluggish growth, and a failed attempt at acquiring Warner Bros. Losing WB to David Ellison’s Paramount was a huge blow — that merger would have given Netflix an easy way to expand its catalog, grow its user base, and build a more established presence in movie theaters. The company now has to navigate those challenges on its own while also figuring out why its current content slate hasn’t resulted in record profits.

snippet: You probably shoudn’t buy a Googlebook. fullText:
You probably shoudn’t buy a Googlebook. That’s less of an opinion about the platform itself, but more about the bad timing that this launch has seen, and protecting your own wallet.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Googlebook as a platform isn’t magically a competitor to Windows and macOS. Rather, it inhabits nearly the exact same space in the market that Chromebook did. The app gap hasn’t been fixed, nor has Google managed to build a platform that someone can go without the deep ecosystems that the dominant players have built out for decades.

If a Chromebook wasn’t for you, Googlebook isn’t either

Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it

There are any number of reasons I could give you not to buy a Googlebook right now. The price tags. The lack of apps. The simple fact that this is a brand new platform you shouldn’t fork over hundreds of dollars to beta test. But, ultimately, I think the biggest reason you shouldn’t be buying a Googlebook is timing.

	

RAMageddon is in full swing, thanks in no small part to Google and its AI competitors, and consumers are paying the price for it. Everything has gotten extraordinarily expensive, and it’s not slowing down anytime soon. Price hikes will continue, and you’re only going to feel the strain more and more. 

With that in mind, why would anyone spend their money on a Googlebook?

That’s really what I’ve been wrestling with the past few weeks in the midst of Google’s big push. Googlebook is asking you to spent $1,000, give or take, on a laptop that’s not fully capable because… it works with your phone? Truly, I just cannot fathom making that choice when you could pay the same, if not less, for a Windows laptop or a MacBook.

From my HP Googlebook 14 review earlier this week:

Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price…

Imagine a scenario. You spend $1,000 or more on a Googlebook today because, right now, it fits your needs. You could have bought a MacBook Air for just a little more, or a Lenovo laptop for a little less. But you reason that, for now, the Googlebook does everything you need it to do. But, six months from now, you pick up a new hobby, change jobs, or have any number of things change that impact what you need from your tech. Suddenly, that Googlebook might not cut it. The problems Googlebook has today are not going to be solved in six months; many, if not all, of the limitations you face today will still exist.

That’s my reasoning for why I won’t buy a Googlebook. What do you think?

title: Spotify says yes, it is busting people for using Family Plan sharing too widely
snippet: Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström confirmed on this week's earnings call that the company is trying to catch Spotify Family plan users who don't actually live together with a new QR code verification method that requires scanning the plan manager's phone. TechCrunch reports that in response to a question about the "crackdown," he called it a "routine improvement" instead: This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty signi … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Stevie Bonifield

 

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström confirmed on this week’s earnings call that the company is trying to catch Spotify Family plan users who don’t actually live together with a new QR code verification method that requires scanning the plan manager’s phone. TechCrunch reports that in response to a question about the “crackdown,” he called it a “routine improvement” instead:

This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base.

As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.

This isn’t the first time Spotify has tried to limit sharing Family plans, which it says are only for people living in the same household. The new QR code verification method has forced some users to get creative to stay on their shared Premium subscriptions — the code refreshes every few seconds and anyone who misses the seven-day window to scan it gets banned from joining a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months.

title: Anthropic takes on ChatGPT Dots and Meta Muse with Claude Duet
snippet: Anthropic is introducing a new AI assistant that can proactively manage tasks across connected apps, keep track of emails and calendars, and continue working even when the app is closed. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Anthropic is introducing a new AI assistant that can proactively manage tasks across connected apps, keep track of emails and calendars, and continue working even when the app is closed. Here are the details.

’A proactive agent that understands what needs your attention’

Anthropic today announced Claude Duet, an always-on AI agent currently rolling out as a research preview to Pro and Max subscribers in the US, with access gradually rolling out via a waitlist.

The feature is included at no additional cost, but counts toward existing plan usage limits, including work performed in the background, which the company notes could cause users to reach those limits “sooner than with chat alone.”

Here’s Anthropic on its new proactive AI assistant:

Claude Duet is a research preview of Claude that you message the way you’d message a person. Tell it what you need, typed or spoken, and it works in the apps you’ve connected, lets you know when something needs you, and is designed to ask before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything.

The company says invitations will go out in waves and adds that “Claude Duet isn’t available on Team or Enterprise plans yet,” though it plans to expand availability to those subscriptions in the future.

We’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent.

It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. pic.twitter.com/kt8gAbWuX8

— Claude (@claudeai) October 21, 2026

Anthropic says that Claude Duet uses the same memories, skills, and connectors as regular Claude, and can even search past conversations so users don’t have to repeat themselves.

Claude Duet runs on its own cloud-based computer, allowing it to continue working even after users close the app.

Additionally, Claude Duet offers integrations with Stripe to check for unpaid invoices and draft payment reminders, as well as Link and Shop Pay to make purchases with user approval.

Here are a few use cases described by Anthropic:

Message it like a person. Type a message or record a voice message. Your main thread stays in one place, so Claude Duet picks up where you left off. You can also start separate channels for different topics, and they share the same memory.

Start the day with a brief. Each morning, it looks across your email and calendar, picks what most needs your attention, and can start the first steps, like drafting replies for you to review. Through the day, it sends updates on the work it’s doing and follows up on threads that have gone quiet.

Hand it larger jobs. Describe what you need, and it works out which apps to use and how much effort the job takes. Bigger results come back as files you can review and edit, such as a research brief, a financial model, a slide deck, or a dashboard. Finished work appears in the Make tab.

Add plugins. Claude Duet supports plugins, such as the small business plugin, and can suggest ones that fit your work.

Use websites without a connector. For sites that don’t have a connector, Claude Duet uses its own browser in the cloud.

According to Claude Duet’s support page, the assistant also has a dedicated Tasks tab where users can track ongoing work and see which tasks need their attention.

Claude Duet also sends updates to the main conversation when a task is completed or requires a decision. Importantly, only users can mark tasks as finished.

Anthropic says Claude Duet is powered by Claude Opus 5.5 and is available through standalone apps for iOS and Android, as well as on the web at claude.ai, for users who receive an invitation.

title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
snippet: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
fullText:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.

Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.

That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.

“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said. 

Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”

Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.

OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

		Lucas is a senior writer at TechCrunch, where he covers artificial intelligence, consumer tech, and startups. He previously covered AI and cybersecurity at Gizmodo. 
You can contact Lucas by emailing [email protected].

title: Iron Man himself now officially endorses Snap’s latest smart glasses
snippet: Snap Specs are available for pre-order now, and actor Robert Downey Jr. is joining the team after he said he “was absolutely sold on Specs within 40 seconds.” more…
fullText:
Snap Specs are available for pre-order now, and actor Robert Downey Jr. is joining the team after he said he “was absolutely sold on Specs within 40 seconds.”

That makes Robert Downey Jr. the latest big-name partnership from Snap, as the company gets ready to launch its first true consumer-ready smart glasses, simply called Specs. Downey Jr. join the team at Snap as the honorary Chief Customer Experience Officer (CCEO), putting him in charge of showing the world just how close to his Iron Man roots these glasses really are.

Downey Jr. launched a new series of videos on the Snap YouTube channel, helping showcase all the cool things Specs can do. From helping you paint better with an AR overlay to watching movies in bed, and even letting Specs calculate where you need to hit the ball on a putting green, Downey Jr. is pulling out all the stops to get you interested in these $2,200 smart glasses.

Snap is clearly challenging Meta’s market leadership in the XR category with a product that combines elements of Meta Ray-Ban Display Glasses and the upcoming Meta VR Glasses. Specs are a completely standalone pair of smart glasses with displays in each lens, plus full hand-tracking support that’s typically only found on a bulkier VR headset.

	

Snap has been building up to the Specs release since 2016 (not a typo). The company has released several experimental developer-only smart glasses during that time, all of which were significantly bulkier than Specs now looks, with huge improvements between each generation.

In addition to the clear Iron Man nod, Snap has also partnered with HBO to launch a Specs Harry Potter experience to coincide with the new HBO show, plus an official partnership with the NBA. The first original episode of Downey Jr.’s SPECS-focused videos will debut during Game 1 of the World Series on Friday, October 23. You can preorder Specs from Snap right now.

title: New iPhone Duo? Here are 4 Features You Should Check Out Now
snippet: A handful of neat capabilities help Apple’s foldable phone feel even more intuitive.
fullText:
If you’ve managed to snag a shiny new iPhone Duo, congratulations on surviving the scramble to get one. Now the fun begins.

I’ve spent a little over a week with Apple’s first foldable phone, and it has several features that make it feel like a genuinely practical and intuitive device — and with a $1,999 starting price, I’d sure hope so. 

What stands out about the Duo is its versatility. Similar to other passport-size folding phones like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold, you can hop between a more compact, 5.4-inch cover screen when sending a text or checking a notification and a wider, 7.6-inch inner display when watching videos, multitasking or scrolling through social media. It’s like a phone-tablet hybrid that fits neatly into a pocket or the palm of your hand. 

		

			

Details like the matte inner display, which minimizes glare and makes the crease less noticeable, along with seamless software integration across screens give the Duo a distinct character of its own.

Here are four features worth checking out to get the most of your new iPhone Duo. And if you’re still in the market for one, it’s worth checking out carrier and trade-in deals to help bring down the cost (and maybe get the phone earlier than January).

Use Duo Preview and Smart Take for photos

Smart Take and Duo Preview can make taking photos a little easier.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo’s foldable design and dual screens open up more ways to take pictures. A few handy features let you easily use the 48-megapixel rear cameras for better shots than you’d get with the 12-megapixel cover-screen selfie camera.

If someone is taking a picture of you or you want to snap a selfie with the rear camera, use Duo Preview to get a glimpse of what the shot will look like. With the phone open, you’ll see an image preview on the cover screen as you or your photographer snaps away, so you can ensure the framing and poses look exactly how you want.

To turn on Duo Preview, unfold the Duo and open the Camera app. Then tap the control in the top left corner (when the phone is in landscape) that looks like a mini Duo. Tap Duo Preview and snap away. 

If you’re trying to take a group photo and there’s no one around to snap it for you, you no longer have to awkwardly prop your phone against a surface and then race against a timer — or make do with a lackluster selfie. Place your Duo on a flat surface when it’s half-folded and point the camera at your subjects. A feature called Smart Take will use AI to detect when everyone is in-frame and ready, and then automatically take a photo. As people change their poses, Smart Take will register that there’s a fresh scene to snap. You can also use Duo Preview to check framing via the cover screen.

To enable Smart Take, open the camera app while the Duo is either opened or closed. Then tap the photo options in the corner (six little dots), and tap Smart Take. A button with a yellow circle will then appear to the right of the shutter; tap that to start the process. 

Smart Take will keep snapping pictures for around two minutes or until it captures about 20 images as people readjust their poses. You’ll then be able to sift through the options in Photos. 

Lastly, Kid Cue can make it easier to hold a child’s attention when snapping photos. With the Duo open, a Snoopy animation will play on the cover screen to draw attention toward the camera. To turn on Kid Cue, unfold the Duo, open the Camera app and tap the Duo icon in the upper left corner. There, you’ll see the option to turn on Kid Cue. 

StandBy mode gets more handy

StandBy on the iPhone Duo works even when the phone isn’t charging.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Apple launched StandBy in 2023, which turns the iPhone into a smart display of sorts, with access to widgets like the clock, calendar and weather. But unlike other iPhones, the Duo doesn’t have to be charging to launch into StandBy. 

Just set the Duo down while it’s locked, either slightly unfolded and on its side in tent mode, or while standing upright. Then you’ll see your favorite widgets, as well as Live Activities. That way, you can track the status of a food delivery, sports score or approaching rideshare at a glance.  

To ensure StandBy is enabled, go to your iPhone’s Settings, then tap StandBy and check that the toggle is on.

Marathon watch as you like

Netflix is optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Streaming video really shines with the iPhone Duo’s dynamic design. Open the phone to watch on the tablet-like, 7.6-inch display. Minimal black bars at the top and bottom of the screen allow for more immersive viewing. 

You can also fold the Duo halfway and set it down, essentially making it look like a mini laptop. With apps like Netflix and Apple TV, your movie or TV show will play on the top half, while controls appear on the bottom for skipping forward, rewinding, pausing, playing and turning on closed captions. Netflix also has an added flair: You’ll see what appears to be a reflection of the upper-screen’s content playing down by the controls, as if it’s subtly mirroring that footage. It makes for a nifty immersive effect.

You can also prop your iPhone Duo into tent mode and watch content on the 5.4-inch cover screen. I do this when I’m moving around my apartment tidying up. That way, I can easily see what’s happening without needing a phone stand. Even though the Duo’s cover screen is significantly smaller than the main display, it’s just big enough to still comfortably watch most content (perhaps not as Christopher Nolan intended, but it’ll do). 

Lock a pair of apps when multitasking

You can lock an app pair when multitasking. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

The iPhone Duo can run up to two apps simultaneously in its open horizontal orientation, so you can watch a YouTube video on one half of your screen while texting your friends on the other, for example. Some other foldable phones support running three apps side-by-side, but I find that feels too crowded. 

On the iPhone Duo, you can save an app pair, so that if you swipe away, you can quickly pull up that same combination without having to drag the apps side by side again. It’s a quick time-saver that lends itself to the intuitive nature of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo.

To create an app pair, tap the divider between two apps that you’ve already dragged side by side. This will lock in that combination, so you can easily restore that dual-window card when you’re scrolling through the App Switcher. Just select the still-paired window and carry on with your multitasking (or doomscrolling).

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Abrar Al-Heeti

title: Beyond the Review: Inside the Onyx RCR 80V
snippet: The Onyx RCR 80V can hit motorcycle speeds, but after hundreds of miles in the saddle, I found there’s a lot more to this compact electric machine than going fast.
fullText:
The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York City, I’m more interested in what it’s like to live with.

The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?

My impression is that Onyx is trying to build a compact electric motorbike with BMX-inspired maneuverability and modern electronics, while leaving owners room to customize it and keep it running. Riding the RCR and talking with founder Tim Seward helped me understand that approach. Whether it holds up over years of ownership is a question a few hundred miles can’t answer.

			

More from CNET

Joseph Kaminski

Onyx RCR 80V GeekBox

Manufacturer figures below are advertised specifications, not independently measured performance results. Prices checked Oct. 14, 2026.

Specification

Onyx RCR 80V

Starting price

$4,699 Street / $4,899 Dual Sport

Motor

Rear hub; advertised 8kW nominal

Battery

Removable 80V, 45Ah / 3.6kWh

Claimed top speed

65–75 mph, depending on configuration; advertised for off-road use

Claimed maximum range

140 miles; current table associates this with Cruise Tune Eco at 15 mph

Claimed acceleration

0–30 mph in 1.7 seconds

Ride modes tested

Eco, Normal, Sport and Hyper

Wheels

17-inch tubeless

Brakes

Hydraulic discs with 220mm rotors

Display

TFT touchscreen

Phone integration

Apple CarPlay / Android Auto

Other features

Reverse, cruise control, regenerative braking, turn signals and alarm/key fob

Advertised ready-to-ride weight

Approximately 155 pounds

Sources: Onyx model and pricing overview⁠, RCR product page⁠, RCR feature page⁠ and Onyx’s brake and wheel description⁠.

Joseph Maldonado

Street, Dual Sport and getting it home

The Street and Dual Sport share the advertised motor and battery ratings. Their clearest hardware differences are the tires and fenders: Street has 4-inch street tires with optional fenders; Dual Sport has 4.5-inch tires with a more aggressive tread and fenders included. See the Onyx model comparison⁠

Neither arrives like a lightweight bicycle. The RCR is a heavy freight delivery that still needs final assembly, and I wouldn’t recommend unpacking it alone. At roughly 155 pounds ready to ride, it also demands some thought about storage before you order.

I live in a three-flight walk-up. That matters more to my daily experience than another few miles per hour at the top end.

Yes, the RCR has pedals. I doubt many people are spending nearly $5,000 because they’re looking forward to using them.

Joseph Maldonado

Small bike, serious performance

I’m 6 feet tall, around 260 pounds and usually carrying a backpack. The RCR has had no trouble moving me around.

Most of my riding has been between 15 and 35 mph, with plenty of time in Normal. I haven’t often felt the need for more. What I appreciate is the reserve power for acceleration and hills, rather than having to ask the bike for everything just to carry a heavier rider.

Seward made a similar point when we talked about the RCR’s development around San Francisco. Steep hills help explain why usable power matters beyond a top-speed claim.

His background also helps explain the bike. An industrial designer whose portfolio includes projects for Sonos and Bird, Seward founded Onyx to bring classic motorbike character to an electric machine. ⁠

He described a combination of motorcycle performance and BMX-style maneuverability. I grew up racing BMX, and I can relate to that influence. The RCR’s compact dimensions make it easy to move around underneath me and maneuver in tighter spaces. Its size is part of its appeal, although the weight is a reminder that this is a very different machine from a BMX bike.

“It’s like a blank canvas that you can customize… It’s not a BMX at all, but it definitely has some influence from when I was a kid,” says Seward.

Joseph Maldonado

The throttle changes the experience

With this much power, how it arrives matters.

On my test bike, Eco and Normal feel smoother and more forgiving. Sport and Hyper respond more immediately to wrist movement. Switching modes changes more than the available speed; it changes how carefully I need to feed in the throttle.

I like having that choice. Sometimes I want an easy cruise. Other times, I appreciate a quicker response. A gentler mode doesn’t eliminate the need for careful throttle control, but it makes the bike’s delivery better suited to how I want to ride.

These impressions apply to the software on my test bike. They aren’t a comparison of Onyx’s newer Cruise and Thrill tunes.

What I can say about range

I haven’t completed a controlled range test, so I don’t have a measured full-charge figure to give you.

What I do have is several hundred miles of use without range anxiety. On one ride from around 151st Street in Harlem to East 26th Street, the display showed a drop of about nine percentage points. My ride took me through Central Park, so we’re looking at about 9 miles. After longer outings through Queens and Brooklyn, I’ve returned with roughly 60% to 70% of the indicated charge remaining.

My much lighter teenage son also rode the RCR on an outing through those boroughs. I recall the indicated charge dropping by 17%, although that wasn’t a controlled comparison with my own riding.

One thing that continues to impress me about the Onyx RCR 80V is just how quiet its motor is. There’s none of that high-pitched whining or wheezing you sometimes hear from electric motors. Power delivery is equally impressive, remaining smooth and consistent whether I’m accelerating from a standstill or riding at higher speeds. I’ve also noticed how much the route itself can affect battery consumption. On a recent commute from 151st Street to East 26th Street, I took a different route instead of traveling entirely through Central Park and used just 6% of the battery compared with 9% on a previous ride. It’s a good reminder that real-world range isn’t simply about distance. Terrain, elevation changes, traffic, speed and riding conditions all influence how efficiently the bike uses energy.

Joseph Maldonado

Those readings describe what I saw on the display. They don’t establish that each percentage point equals a mile, or that the bike will travel 100 miles on a charge. Without recorded distances, consistent conditions and a fuller discharge test, that would be an extrapolation.

Rider weight, speed, acceleration and terrain all matter. My conclusion is narrower: the battery has comfortably covered the rides I’ve taken. Someone spending more time at high speed should expect a different experience.

Onyx itself recommends watching battery voltage for a better indication of remaining charge and range. That’s another reason to treat my percentage readings as observations rather than precision measurements. See ONYX battery guidance⁠

Joseph Maldonado

Comfortable suspension, with limits at the seat

The RCR fits me surprisingly well, and the suspension has done a good job taking the edge off New York’s potholes and broken pavement.

The seat is comfortable with good cushioning for shorter rides. After about 90 minutes, though, I start shifting around. The suspension helps with the road underneath me, but it doesn’t eliminate the discomfort that builds during a longer ride. That also could be due to my size; I’m far from a lightweight. 

The brakes have also felt consistently strong. After a few hundred miles, lever travel still feels close to how it did at the start, and I haven’t noticed a meaningful decline in stopping performance. That’s a riding impression, not a measured stopping-distance or brake-wear test.

Cruise control and reverse were pleasant surprises

Cruise control sounded like a minor convenience until I used it. On the inclines I’ve encountered with it engaged, the RCR has held the selected speed even with my weight aboard. That has been a more useful demonstration of its available power than a top-speed run.

Discovering that it could also reverse was another pleasant surprise. On a machine this heavy, powered reverse is a feature I’m glad to have. Onyx documents both functions in its advanced controls guide.

Joseph Maldonado

CarPlay is a favorite feature — and a frustration

I didn’t expect to care this much about CarPlay. Having navigation and audio controls on the built-in display means I can leave my phone put away.

My main complaint is what happens to the motorbike’s own information. While using CarPlay, especially during a call, I want speed and battery status to remain easy to see. On my test bike, they aren’t presented as conveniently as I’d like.

Onyx told me it intends to address the display issue through a software update.

Navigation brings up another issue. I’d like routing that better reflects the vehicle I’m riding. Because it uses CarPlay, it offers driving directions. However, I would like the option to choose a different route if I choose to.

“Having Android Auto and CarPlay in the bike makes me want to ride more… Part of the new update will show stats like battery level and mode on the side while using it,” says Seward, who is also Onyx’s chief design officer.

Joseph Maldonado

Signals, lights and wet pavement

The turn signals sit close to the body, with less protruding hardware to catch on something. I like that design, but in sunny settings, the signals may not be as visible.

They don’t self-cancel. The display indicators help, but I’d prefer automatic cancellation to discovering I’ve announced a left turn for the last 20 blocks (minor complaint). The Bluetooth connection indicator is another small, useful display detail.

The headlight has worked well for the nighttime riding I’ve done. The halo running light and main beam give the bike a distinctive look, with high beam available when needed.

Joseph Maldonado

I’ve also ridden in the rain and on wet pavement without noticing handling problems. That’s limited experience, not a comprehensive wet-weather test. The more immediate issue is spray, as my bike doesn’t have the optional fenders installed, and New York street water gets everywhere.

Fenders are high on my list before doing more wet-weather riding.

Tubeless tires and everyday maintenance

The tubeless setup matters to me because removing a motorized rear wheel to deal with a flat tube can become a project. I’d rather avoid that extra complication where possible.

Tubeless doesn’t mean puncture-proof, and I wouldn’t assume any roadside plug is a permanent repair suitable for motorcycle speeds. But it’s a great go-to when in a pinch. Not having to remove the wheel to make it to your destination is clutch. 

“These are basically motorcycle wheels and tires, so if you get a nail, you can patch or plug it without taking the wheel off and replacing the whole tube,” says Seward.

Joseph Kaminski

Forget the fob and the bike stays put

I’ve kept the RCR in storage at my partner’s apartment because she has an elevator. I sometimes forget to leave the key fob with it, which works well until I arrive without the fob.

That experience made phone or NFC access more appealing. Seward told me Onyx is developing app-based diagnostics, firmware updates and service support, and we discussed possible phone access. I’d welcome it, along with integrated tracking or movement alerts.

For now, I keep an AirTag hidden in the bike. I’ve also found the rear-wheel locking behavior reassuring when the bike is secured, although that isn’t a substitute for a physical lock.

Onyx already links a Superpower BMS app for battery monitoring. That should be distinguished from the broader app and unlocking features we discussed; I haven’t established that those proposed functions are available. See the Onyx product page

Joseph Maldonado

⁠

The pedals don’t settle the legal question

I think of the RCR as a compact electric motorcycle. That description doesn’t, by itself, establish whether a particular example can be registered for road use. But it can be insured.

New York’s legal definition of an electric-assist bicycle includes a motor below 750 watts and specified assistance-speed limits. The RCR’s advertised power and performance exceed those limits. Buyers shouldn’t assume that pedals or a lower-speed setting make it a legal e-bike. See New York DMV definitions⁠

I haven’t verified New York registration eligibility for this exact model and configuration. That needs to be resolved with the DMV and the manufacturer before it can be presented as a straightforward street-legal commuting option. Bicycle lanes and walking routes should not be assumed available to it.

Joseph Maldonado

Beyond the ride: A conversation with Tim Seward

Seward’s explanation of Onyx starts with the products he no longer wanted to design. During our conversation, he described working on consumer electronics for brands including Sonos, HP and Samsung, only to watch products become disposable shortly after reaching the market. His experiences with furniture and old gas-powered mopeds suggested a different approach.

The following excerpts are edited for length and clarity from the interview transcript. Questions have been shortened, and the discussion has been reordered by topic. Future features are plans described during the interview, not confirmation that they are available today.

Joseph Maldonado

Question: Is there anything about your background or the bike that people might not know?

Seward: Before Onyx, I was a big consumer-electronics designer. I worked on Sonos, HP, Samsung, and all sorts of products you would see at Best Buy. While I liked that job, I didn’t like that people were throwing away their products.

When I was customizing gas-powered mopeds, I realized I was working on vehicles 30 to 50 years old. Who knows how many hands it went through until it got to me? I was like, I need to make products like this. I need to make products that, even if Onyx dies tomorrow, the products will live on. I didn’t want to continue to create landfill.

Joseph Maldonado

Question: If an owner keeps this bike for five years, what can they realistically expect for battery health?

Seward: With our extra layer of health protections, we are confident our battery pack will show only a 10% degradation in 10 years. So, at the five-year mark, you won’t even notice much of a difference, if any, in performance.

(That’s an ambitious prediction. Seward’s response didn’t include the testing, charging habits or usage conditions behind it, so I wouldn’t treat it as a guaranteed outcome or a warranty. It does give me something specific to follow up on as the bike ages.)

Question: How committed is Onyx to supporting owners with replacement parts years down the road?

Seward: We strive to offer hard-to-find parts even for discontinued products that are 5 to 6 years old. Also, our newest model, the RCR 80V, uses many parts that are compatible with aftermarket upgrades, so you can modify or maintain it for decades to come.

(That gets to one of my biggest questions about an expensive electric vehicle: What happens when something breaks after the model is no longer current? Aftermarket compatibility could help keep the RCR running, although it isn’t a guarantee that every component will remain available.)

Joseph Maldonado

Question: What sets Onyx apart from the growing number of electric motorcycle companies?

Seward: We are not just building a bike. We are building a community of riders who support each other across the globe.

(That connects with how I found my way to Onyx. I met John Angel while testing another bike, and he kept encouraging me to try an RCR. Before I spoke with the company, another rider had already shared his experience and got me interested.

The community side matters most when it becomes useful: Someone helping you understand a feature, troubleshoot a problem or figure out a modification. That’s the kind of owner involvement I’d like to see continue as Onyx grows.

Onyx also brings its community together through events like Onyx Week, where owners and enthusiasts participate in organized rides, meet members of the Onyx team, exchange ideas, and connect with other riders. Events have been organized in Los Angeles and New York, giving owners an opportunity to experience the community beyond online discussions and social media.)

Joseph Maldonado

What stays with me

The RCR has more power than I usually need and has covered my outings without battery anxiety. CarPlay and cruise control have become features I actually value. The seat can become less comfortable on longer rides, and the display should show the current speed and battery level while on a call. 

Talking with Seward gave me a clearer understanding of the decisions behind those experiences. Customer feedback helped shape the 80V, while his experience with disposable electronics explains why he wants owners to keep these bikes running.

It’s nice to hear a company talk about making something you can keep for years instead of pushing you to buy a new model every year. That intention still has to be backed by replacement parts, documentation and service. Onyx’s published guidance says it doesn’t repair, refurbish or rebalance batteries, so long-term battery support remains an important question. See Onyx’s battery support policy⁠

For me, that’s what makes this worth looking at beyond the review — understanding why the RCR was built this way, how owners influence what comes next and whether the support can live up to the design. Would I recommend getting one? Heck yeah!

Joseph Maldonado

title: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook could debut on November 6: Here’s what to expect
snippet: After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th. more…
fullText:
After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th.

Of course, rumors are rumors – though essentially every reputable source has aligned on the idea of the MacBook Pro gaining support for touch very shortly. Apple even left a few hints in macOS 27: Touch Support in Sidecar, pull to refresh support, and slightly bigger menu bar items.

One could call all of this a mere coincidence, but it’s probably exactly what it looks like. Regardless, here’s what the first touchscreen MacBook will have to offer.

OLED, Dynamic Island

On the display panel side of things, the redesigned MacBook Pro will come with a Tandem OLED display. This will be similar to the iPad Pro, which is often touted as one of the best mobile displays on the market. Tandem OLED comprises of stacked OLED panels, which allows for incredible colors, strong contrast, and increased brightness.

Reports also suggest it’ll come with a Dynamic Island, and it’ll be a bit smaller than the one on the iPhone. It won’t, however, come with support for Face ID.

Software optimizations

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple will have some special optimizations for the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, beyond what’s already visible in the betas of macOS 27:

“For instance, if users touch a button or control, the interface will bring up a new type of menu surrounding their finger that provides more relevant options for touch commands.

The software will also display the most appropriate set of controls based on users’ prior interaction. And if a person taps an item in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the set of controls will enlarge to be more easily selectable with a finger.”

M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Despite initial reporting suggesting that we’ll be seeing the debut of the M6 Pro and Max in the redesigned MacBook Pro, Apple is now skipping the release of those chips to accelerate the M7. This means that the first iteration of 2nm chips won’t be making their way to the redesigned MacBook Pros, and they’ll instead offer the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

There won’t be a base model version of this computer quite yet, though rumors suggest that Apple will be launching a base version of the redesigned MacBook Pro with an M7 chip as early as next spring.

Slightly thinner chassis, significantly lighter

One design rumor for the new MacBook Pro is the fact that it’ll be slightly slimmer and lighter – though it’s unclear how meaningful this will be. The last MacBook Pro iteration made the computers look and feel quite chunky, so a bit of progress here would likely be welcome – so long as it doesn’t come at the compromise of thermals.

Bloomberg has also reported that these computers will be ‘significantly lighter,’ thanks to re-engineering of internal components.

Release date

	

According to the Power On newsletter, Apple will potentially release these new MacBook Pro models on November 6th, making a straight four weeks of new Apple launches with iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, the new MacBook Pro, and HomeView + Apple TV 4K. 

As of now, there’s no Apple release scheduled for November 6th, so it would make sense to be the new MacBook Pro:

Now, I have a little more to share: Apple is planning to hold a “reset” at its retail stores on the evening of Thursday, Nov. 5, into Friday, Nov. 6, that implies new signage and products will be placed on store tables. Given that this Friday is a week after the Mac announcements (when Apple would typically release products), it would make sense that this is the date when at least some of the new items become available to customers.

snippet: Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover. fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

The through-line in every iPhone Duo review yesterday was this: excellent hardware (though a bit too heavy) and a chaotic software experience. When Apple’s foldable launches on Friday, it will remind early adopters of what Android used to feel like whenever a new form factor was introduced: exciting, janky, and slightly aggravating.

	

I think 9to5Google readers understand that Android is for tweakers. It’s why so many of you sign up for Android betas on daily-driver hardware; it’s why there’s a thriving community of indie developers filling gaps in the ecosystem. Android’s freedom and flexibility (and cost) make it particularly well suited to the cavalcade of use cases and designs we see in the market today.

That openness confers other, more nebulous benefits; it’s far easier to emulate games on Android along with other legally grey activities that won’t be mentioned here. If there’s something you want to do on Android, chances are you can figure out a way to do it.

It seems like the iPhone Duo’s early adopters will be faced with a similar conundrum: the ability to do more on a device that is likely to frustrate and delight in equal measure. As Ben explains in his iPhone Duo review roundup, “the app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet.”

But as with all things iPhone, app and software improvements are likely to come quickly and consistently over the next few months and years. Ben eloquently sums up the situation: “Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start.”

✉️ Inbox

Galaxy S27 might drop to 8GB of RAM; other Android phones could go back to 4GB. Not sure I entirely believe this rumor, but it is true that Google has been making Android more memory-efficient, so maybe it is true?

ModRetro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it? This product feels like the physical manifestation of using X.

Spotify podcast memberships let you support your favorite shows and get added perks. I support this feature, but the continued fragmentation of the podcast subscription ecosystem is driving me crazy.

Iron Man himself now officially endorses Snap’s latest smart glasses. Because he’s the only person who can afford to buy them.

Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji. Depending on who you ask, this is a good thing or a terrible thing.

Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer. Perfect timing with yesterday’s PHP vulnerabilities.

You can cut your cell phone bill to $10/month or get a Pixel 11 for $400 right now – here’s how. Some decent deals from Mint Mobile (#notsponsored).

YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos. This makes sense to me; dislike buttons used to be there to help shape your algorithm, but there are so many other ways to do that today that its existence feels unnecessary.

Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence. I can’t wait to ask Gemini about that mole on my back while driving my in-laws around the city.

Google Maps on CarPlay rolling out Gemini when navigating

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Google gives Pixel 9 another year of free Satellite SOS connectivity. I have a feeling this isn’t the last announcement of this kind we’ll see.

Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you

The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say. This has been a very good year for book-style foldables, and the momentum is slated to continue into 2027.

Google reiterates missing Fitbit Air sleep breathing quality feature coming ‘soon’

Google TV powers the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro glasses, and that’s exactly the problem

Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports

OpenAI GPT models are coming to Google Antigravity ‘soon,’ Cloud ‘in the coming weeks’. OpenAI and Microsoft continue their very public divorce.

Xbox Cloud Gaming’s added playtime costs start at around 40¢ per hour. Who is asking for this feature?

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music. The app may be an iOS clone, but I’m happy it exists.

Non-folding phones can still be interesting

Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price

The real reason to care about Vivo’s latest phone is the camera [Gallery]

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

I was the guest on this week’s Sideload episode, and we talked about my favorite thing: AI. In particular, how we use AI in our daily lives.

One thing we touched on that I’m going to delve into in a future newsletter is whether Google is actually behind the competition with Gemini. With the recent release of Gemini 4 Argon, it’s clear the company is close to the frontier, but the more important question to answer is whether Gemini is a good product. I make the argument that it is, especially because Google has its tendrils in every part of my life, from email to search to maps, and that makes Gemini’s answers far more useful when I ask it questions of a personal nature. That it has a 25% market share right now is almost accidental; so many people are forced to interact with Gemini in one way or another through Google’s various products.

It’s also bizarre that Google hasn’t figured out a way to compete with Meta on the personal agent front. On its earnings call, Meta said that Muse has been used by over 10 million people, and 25% of them use it every day. Google has Spark, but it’s not in the same league in terms of functionality or mindshare.

Google is unquestionably behind Anthropic and OpenAI where the money is made: in the enterprise. Antigravity is a subpar harness, and Argon is a capable but unspectacular coding agent.

Nevertheless, Google has the money, the user base, and, most importantly, the incentive to keep going after the top labs. In an interview this week with Alex Kantrowitz, CEO Sundar Pichai said that he is committed to the frontier at all costs, and that Google Cloud compute capacity is being reallocated in 2027 to train state-of-the-art models.

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s proactive AI agent answer to Muse and OpenAI’s Dots

It’s almost Thanksgiving travel season, which means it’s time to re-up one of the best Onion videos about the places our souls go to die: airports.

As mentioned above, Supernatural is relaunching on the Quest as a new independent app with the original owners and much of the same crew. When Meta announced that it was laying off much of its Reality Labs division and shutting Supernatural down, it didn’t look good for the future of what I consider the best VR workout app ever made. But by the summer, it was announced that Meta had negotiated a sale of the brand and IP (but not the code), which allowed the formation of Supernatural Health.

Launching this week in Early Access, it’s now double what it used to cost — $200 a year — but it’s one of the few subscriptions I look forward to paying. If you’re a Quest owner, I cannot recommend it highly enough.

title: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught
snippet: The company is looking to roll out the gold two-seater robotaxis to other U.S. cities this year, even as it goes mum on the number of paid rides.
fullText:
Tesla says it is preparing to launch its shiny gold Cybercab in new markets outside its home of Austin, Texas, in a bid to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation.” 

“We’re starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth,” Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday.

Tesla has previously shown a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle it calls the “Robovan,” but it’s unclear if Taneja’s bombastic comments mean the company is working on other types of transportation.

What was clearer on the call is that Tesla’s Cybercab expansion will begin in Dallas next month and spread to other cities by the end of this year. Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The company also said on its earnings call that it will start selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year.

Broader expansion of the Cybercab could set up a real fight with Waymo, which is currently the market leader for robotaxis in the United States, with more than 4,000 of them deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should allow it to undercut Waymo and other robotaxi operators on price. But the company has to reach real scale outside Austin in order to prove that point.

Tesla said it’s ready thanks to a dramatic increase in the number of miles its self-driving cars have traveled in recent weeks. While that may be true, Tesla was mum on Wednesday about how much money the overall robotaxi effort is bringing in. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won’t be noticeable in the company’s overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, “and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.”

Tesla also made a change to its letter to shareholders that further obscures what little visibility there was into its robotaxi business.

In Tesla’s second-quarter letter, the company included a chart for “Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles.” A close read of that chart showed a 36% decline from the first quarter of the year. In the new letter released on Wednesday, Tesla changed that chart to show “Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles” — an indicator of how far the fleet cars are driving, whether or not they have paying riders on board.

There wasn’t much more clarity on the call, either. When asked about paid robotaxi miles traveled, Taneja said the company is “seeing utilization improving,” but didn’t offer specifics.

Instead, Taneja kept most of his comments generally focused on Tesla’s plans to scale the Cybercab. That included praise for Tesla’s engineering team for creating a vehicle that, according to the manufacturing team, is very easy to build — and build quickly.

“They think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,” he said. “So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.” 

What might be a challenge, Taneja said, is that Tesla needs to make sure it has “all the regulatory approvals” so it can “start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.” That echoes many previous comments from Musk, who has long claimed that “regulatory approval” was the biggest barrier to Tesla’s robotaxi plans, not technical progress.

Musk has always been a bit hazy about what approvals, specifically, he felt were needed. The company has run into a regulatory hurdle this year, though. In September, just hours after Tesla formally launched its Cybercab in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with current federal motor vehicle safety standards.

All automakers self-certify that their vehicles conform to these standards, and Tesla has claimed that the Cybercab is compliant. But it is missing features that the current standards require, like a brake pedal and side mirrors. The NHTSA has proposed removing some of these requirements, but that rule change is likely still at least a few months away.

Not every Tesla executive agreed on this during Wednesday’s call.

Asked about the remaining bottlenecks for a wider robotaxi rollout, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president overseeing autonomy, said they are “not purely regulatory.” 

“It’s technology-driven,” he said. “We had initially had the robotaxi service from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., and then expanded to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m, now it’s going to be pretty soon, [to] 2 a.m. So we’re slowly expanding the availability of robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software.”

That could be why Tesla’s service still doesn’t operate on highways, and in certain conditions, although it has been spotted operating in heavy rain many times in Austin — something Waymo’s robotaxis have largely avoided. Elluswamy said Wednesday that Tesla plans to tackle more of these challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year, before scaling further. 

“We just want to make sure that there’s not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there’s the slightest possible risk at all, we don’t like to take on that risk,” he said.

title: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback
snippet: Oura alleges in its newest lawsuit that Ultrahuman's Ring Pro infringes two of its patents.
fullText:
Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn.

In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring.

Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market. The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year.

“Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.”

Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing.

One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart-ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors.

Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S.

Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations.

“Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.”

Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air.

Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung, RingConn, Circular, and Zepp Health. Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products.

The dispute emerges as the smart-ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors.

The lawsuit also comes just weeks after Oura shelved its $2.2 billion IPO, citing “uncertainty” in the market. The company has continued to add features to its smart rings, introducing new fitness metrics earlier this week that help users track how workouts affect their cardiovascular health.

In September, Ultrahuman raised $70 million from investors including Qualcomm Ventures and Labcorp, valuing the startup at about $365 million. The startup is also working with Qualcomm on a new smart ring that could run more software directly on the device, as it looks to expand beyond health and fitness tracking into areas such as AI interactions and gaming.

The article has been updated to include comments from Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar.

title: Walmart’s $60 Google TV streamer might be the only good deal left in streaming
snippet: As prices skyrocket on virtually everything else, Walmart’s $60 Onn 4K Pro streamer with Google TV might be the only good deal left — if you can find it in stock. more…
fullText:
As prices skyrocket on virtually everything else, Walmart’s $60 Onn 4K Pro streamer with Google TV might be the only good deal left — if you can find it in stock.

Prices on streaming hardware have exploded in recent months. Just a few examples include:

Google TV Streamer: Was $99, now $149

Apple TV 4K: Was $129, now $299 (new model)

Nvidia Shield TV Pro: Was $199, now $299

Roku Ultra: Was $100, now $150

It’s rough out there folks. AI is totally worth it, right?

Anyway, all of those price hikes have had me revisiting the Walmart Onn 4K Pro that launched earlier this year and that I’ve been using in one of the rooms in my house for the past few months. Put simply, it gets the job done very well, and is a tremendous deal compared to everything around it.

	

The most direct comparison to the Onn 4K Pro is the Google TV Streamer, and they are pretty close across the board. They have virtually identical software, though Google’s first-party release obviously gets updates and new features a bit quicker. Performance is also nearly identical, with the only big difference being 4GB of RAM in Google’s streamer vs 3GB in Walmart’s. Most of the time, it doesn’t matter.

Walmart’s streamer continues to be a good performer day-in and day-out, and there are little things I actually prefer over Google’s. Topping that list would be the remote, which is a bit more comfortable and backlit, the latter being invaluable in a dark room at night. I could do without the slightly obnoxious “Free TV” button, but I’m overall quite happy with the remote, and even more so with the find remote button on top of the actual streaming box.

					

Google TV on a speedy set-top box with solid hardware and a good remote, all for $60. It’s the best deal in streaming, enough said!

					

				

Pros

				

											

Enough horsepower for speedy Google TV performance

											

Comfortable, backlit remote

											

Plenty of ports

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Hard to find in stock

											

Fabric is hard to clean if it gets dirty

									

			

			

The hardware itself is unassuming with a fabric top and a footprint similar to any other streaming box. That fabric top won’t be a problem for most but, crazy tip, don’t spill anything on it! It’s basically impossible to clean if it gets dirty.

As far as ports go, you’ve got HDMI, Ethernet, full-size USB-A, and the whole thing draws power from USB-C instead of a barrel plug like the last generation — dreams do come true!

	

All of that comes together for just $60. It’s nothing ground-breaking, sure, but this is just a good streamer in every meaningful way without costing an arm and a leg like virtually everything else does right now. The biggest headache is just finding the thing in stock. We’ve been tracking stock for months and, finally, Walmart seems to be more consistently selling Onn 4K Pro both in stores and online, but your results may still vary depending on when you go to buy and where you live. 

Onn 4K Pro at Walmart

If you can’t find the Pro, Walmart also has its Onn 4K Plus dongle that costs just $50 and, in most ways, matches up with the Pro. The main things you’re giving up are the Ethernet port, USB-A port, and a bit of performance.
