title: Apple and DOJ notify court of impasse over document cutoff in antitrust lawsuit
snippet: Apple and the Department of Justice have submitted a joint notice of impasse over how recent Apple’s documents must be to fall within the scope of discovery in their ongoing antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and the Department of Justice have submitted a joint notice of impasse over how recent Apple’s documents must be to fall within the scope of discovery in their ongoing antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details.

A bit of context

In March 2024, the Department of Justice, alongside 15 states and the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of illegally maintaining a monopoly in the smartphone market.

In essence, they accuse Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case. Interestingly, Apple and the DOJ have also reportedly been engaged in settlement talks behind the scenes.

Back to the disputes, they have included how many Apple employees’ records should be searched, whether Apple must produce documents from outside the US, and Apple’s efforts to obtain records from 14 federal agencies, which the government continues to challenge.

Amid these disputes, the discovery schedule has been extended several times, which brings us to today’s filing.

Apple and DOJ at odds over document production cutoff

In a joint notice filed today, Apple and the DOJ inform the court of “an impasse concerning

the cutoff date for Apple’s productions in response to all Requests for Production.”

According to the DOJ, while the two sides initially agreed to a June 20, 2025 cutoff for the documents Apple would be required to produce, that date was based on the original discovery schedule, which has since been pushed back.

In practical terms, the June 20, 2025 cutoff date was agreed upon with the expectation that fact discovery would be completed by July 31, 2026. However, that deadline has since been extended twice, and is now scheduled for late May 2027.

As a result, the DOJ argues that Apple should be required to update its document production to include records created up to 30 days before fact discovery closes, warning that sticking to the original cutoff could prevent the government from obtaining evidence of Apple’s allegedly “ongoing anticompetitive conduct.”

Plaintiffs contend they should not be prejudiced in obtaining and presenting evidence of Apple’s ongoing anticompetitive conduct by the extended fact discovery schedule, particularly when Apple requested the delay. Plaintiffs believe that Apple’s proposal to consider supplementation on a case-by-case basis is unworkable, likely to generate more disputes over the course of fact discovery, and inconsistent with Apple’s duty to supplement under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e).

Apple, on the other hand, argues that the June 2025 cutoff was part of a negotiated agreement and that the DOJ’s request would effectively restart the document discovery process, introducing “months of delay into this case.”

The parties previously agreed to a presumptive June 20, 2025 discovery cut-off. Apple then substantially completed its document productions in the Government Action in 12 months — with a massive investment of resources and hundreds of contractors dedicated to the process. Re-collecting from 54 custodians and numerous other sources, then searching, reviewing, and producing new materials for a 22-month period would take Apple several more months. It is simply not feasible for Apple to produce documents up until 30 days before the close of fact discovery, as that would mean new collections, searches, review, and production within those last 30 days, after almost all depositions will be complete.”

Instead, Apple says it is willing to consider targeted requests for additional documents on a case-by-case basis, an approach the DOJ argues would be unworkable and likely lead to further disputes.

Apple also disputed the DOJ’s suggestion that the company was solely responsible for the schedule extensions and pointed out that the government has yet to produce documents in response to most of Apple’s requests, which were “served over 15 months ago.”

title: Apple still makes it too hard for Apple Pay competitors to emerge, says UK
snippet: Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay … more…
fullText:
Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay …

When Apple first started embedding an NFC chip in iPhones to enable contactless payment, only the Apple Wallet app could take advantage of this. Third-party apps could use the NFC chip for other purposes, but not for card payments.

That saw the iPhone maker facing antitrust action in multiple countries around the world. In a number of them, it’s been forced to unlock access to the chip, most notably in the EU.

In EU countries, developers can request an entitlement to get access by proving to Apple that they meet the industry standards and hold the licenses needed to process consumer payments. No fees are payable. Users are then allowed to choose the default wallet app that appears when they double-click the side button or hold their phone near a payment terminal. 

In the UK, however, the CMA told Reuters that Apple hasn’t offered developers the same terms. 

CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said […] “We have ​heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.”

	

Accordingly, the regulator has opened a public consultation on its proposed loosening of Apple’s grip on the contactless payment chip. Apple has responded by rejecting the proposal, but saying that it will continue to work with the CMA.

“We do ⁠not ​believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an ​approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome ​that is in the best interest of our users.”

9to5Mac’s Take

I see this very much like third-party app stores. While I understand Apple’s position, the company is ultimately likely to lose these battles and is showing no sign of skating to where the regulatory puck is headed.

It seems a needless battle given that the commercial risk to Apple is very limited – the vast majority of iPhone owners are exceedingly unlikely to change the defaults for either app store or wallet app when given the choice.

title: MacBook Neo helps Apple soften the blow of global PC market downturn, per report
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report on global PC shipments for Q3 2026 shows Apple outperforming the broader market, with the MacBook Neo helping cushion the impact of declining demand. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report on global PC shipments for Q3 2026 shows Apple outperforming the broader market, with the MacBook Neo helping cushion the impact of declining demand. Here are the details.

In a new report released today, Counterpoint Research says global PC shipments plunged 21% during Q3 2026, compared with the year-ago period.

In absolute numbers, Counterpoint says global shipments totaled 57 million units, with Lenovo leading the market with a 26.3% share, despite a 23% year-over-year decline.

HP held second place with an 18.1% share and a 31% decline in shipments, followed by Dell (13.3% share, down 25%), Apple (9.8% share, down 11%), and ASUS, which rounded out the top five with a 9.2% share and a 7% decline. Other vendors accounted for the remaining 23.3% of the market, with shipments down 16% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for the quarter:

“Apple’s shipments declined 11% YoY to 5.6 million units, giving it a 9.8% market share, up from 8.7% a year earlier. The MacBook Neo helped cushion the decline, allowing Apple to outperform the overall market.”

Commenting on the results, Counterpoint Research senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that Apple and ASUS outperformed the broader market “through differentiated product portfolios and competitive positioning.”

As most 9to5Mac readers are probably guessing by now, rising memory and other component costs were major contributors to the market-wide downturn. Counterpoint says higher PC prices discouraged consumers from upgrading their devices and weakened demand across the industry.

According to Counterpoint’s data, contract prices for 8GB DDR4 RAM modules rose 24% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, while 1TB NVMe SSD prices increased 29%.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects RAM prices to rise another 13% in Q4 and 15% in Q1 2027, while SSD prices are projected to increase 11% in Q4 before stabilizing in early 2027.

iOS 27.2 is coming next week and brings two new features for Apple TV subscribers. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Profiles come to iPhone and iPad, and with new characters

Apple TV is currently the only major streaming service that doesn’t offer user profiles on iPhone and iPad. But that’s about to change with iOS and iPadOS 27.2.

Profiles already exist in tvOS for big-screen viewing of Apple TV content, but now they’re coming to Apple’s other platforms too.

When you create user profiles on one platform, they automatically sync to others, letting you keep playback history, queues, and recommendations all personalized for each viewer. And if you set up a profile for your child, they’ll only see age-appropriate Apple TV content.

Alongside the expansion of profiles to more platforms, Apple has added a variety of new profile image options in iOS 27.2. Characters from Apple TV kids’ series like The Snoopy Show, Frog and Toad, and Stillwater are all now available.

Apple TV is taking accessibility a step beyond subtitle options by adding official support for sign language on select movies and shows.

With iOS 27.2, users can optionally enable American Sign Language (ASL) or British Sign Language (BSL).

You’ll find the option to enable sign language inside the Settings app under Apps ⇾ TV ⇾ Sign Language. It’s unknown how many Apple TV titles will support sign language initially, but it’s great to see the feature added.

title: Following $5.7B verdict, Taction wants a cut of iPhone and Apple Watch sales through 2035
snippet: Following a historic $5.7 billion patent infringement verdict against Apple, Taction Technology is now seeking additional damages, interest, and ongoing royalties on future iPhone and Apple Watch sales. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following a historic $5.7 billion patent infringement verdict against Apple, Taction Technology is now seeking additional damages, interest, and ongoing royalties on future iPhone and Apple Watch sales. Here are the details.

Taction seeks additional compensation

Late last month, a US jury found that Apple’s Taptic Engine infringed on two patents held by Taction Technology, awarding $5.7 billion in damages. Apple strongly disputed the verdict, arguing that its technology was fundamentally different from Taction’s, and said it would appeal.

A few weeks later, Apple asked the court to overturn the verdict or order a new trial, arguing that Taction had failed to provide evidence supporting the $5.7 billion award, leaving jurors to engage in “impermissible guesswork on a massive scale.”

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Taction has filed a motion seeking supplemental damages, ongoing royalties on future iPhone and Apple Watch sales, prejudgment interest dating back to April 2021, and additional interest from the date of the final judgment until Apple pays.

According to Taction, the jury’s award only accounted for Apple’s sales through March 2026, leaving another six months of iPhone and Apple Watch sales for which the company is now seeking compensation.

Interestingly, Taction is using Apple’s own arguments from its previous patent litigation against Samsung to support its request for ongoing royalties.

In that case, Apple argued that royalties should apply not only to products found to infringe its patents, but also to newer models using essentially the same technology.

Taction is now making the same argument, seeking to extend royalty payments to Apple’s latest devices, including the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4, which it says “are not more than colorably different from the infringing products.”

	

From the filing:

Apple itself has embraced this rule. As a patentee seeking ongoing royalties, Apple told the Northern District of California that “any ongoing royalties extend not only to ongoing sales of products found to infringe by the jury, but also to products ‘not more than colorably different’ therefrom.”

For the ongoing payments on what Taction claims are infringing products, the company is asking the court to compel Apple to provide quarterly reports of its US sales, with royalty payments due within 30 days of the end of each quarter.

Taction is proposing a 7% annual rate for prejudgment interest under California law. The company is also asking the court to extend royalty payments through September 24, 2035, when the patents in question are set to expire.

One important caveat to keep in mind: the judge has yet to enter the jury’s verdict as a final judgment, so the original $5.7 billion award and Taction’s additional demands remain unresolved, as does Apple’s motion to overturn the verdict or secure a new trial.

title: Fitbit Edge doesn’t have Google Wallet because ‘less than 1%’ of Charge owners used it
snippet: Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature. more…
fullText:
Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature.

The ability to pay at the register with your wearable is nothing new, but NFC support on smartwatches and trackers has been pretty hit or miss in the past. Google supports the feature as a standard across the Pixel Watch lineup, and the last-gen Fitbit Charge 6 also supported the feature.

But, with the new Fitbit Edge, NFC support is gone and, in turn, so is Google Wallet.

It’s an interesting regression on Google’s part, so why the change? In a statement to Android Authority, Google explains that it really just comes down to a lack of people actually using this feature on the Fitbit Charge 6. 

	

Fitbit Edge does not offer NFC for payments. It was not widely used by our Charge 6 users — in fact, less than 1% reported using the feature on Charge 6 — so we prioritized other top features such as adding an altimeter and requested improvements.

Google says that skipping NFC left room to “prioritize” other features such as the Edge’s new altimeter, but it still seems like a shame to skip out on mobile payments for what is very much a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

	

Would you have used Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge? Is it a dealbreaker? Let us know in the comments below.

Fitbit Edge launches on October 27, with pre-orders open now.

title: Apple reportedly boosts iPhone Duo orders by more than 40% given strong demand
snippet: Supply chain reports suggest that Apple has increased iPhone Duo orders by more than 40% in response to what the company described as “extraordinary” pre-order demand. Delivery dates started slipping literally within a minute or so of pre-orders opening, and it wasn’t immediately clear whether this reflected high demand or poor supply. fullText:
Supply chain reports suggest that Apple has increased iPhone Duo orders by more than 40% in response to what the company described as “extraordinary” pre-order demand.

Delivery dates started slipping literally within a minute or so of pre-orders opening, and it wasn’t immediately clear whether this reflected high demand or poor supply. This latest report seems to point firmly to the former … 

Pre-orders opened on Friday and customers immediately reported receiving extended delivery dates, some of them into late January. Apple said that this was due to what it described as “extraordinary” demand for its first folding iPhone, but this is a phrase it frequently uses for new iPhone launches. The company also limited orders to a maximum of two per customer in a bid to tackle scalping.

As we expected, some of those ordering the new iPhone were subsequently given earlier estimated shipping dates. This may be explained by a DigiTimes report based on supply chain sources suggesting that Apple has ramped up production.

The report indicates that Apple expects strong demand to continue, and has boosted its shipment targets from 9.7 million to 14 million units over the first 12 months.

Early customers are going to have to contend with third-party apps not yet optimized for the device, but Apple says the situation is improving rapidly as developers get on board. The first reviews based on a week of usage present a consistent view, with app support one of five key takeouts.

The downgrade to Touch ID was another of these, but a report today says Apple is already testing iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID.

snippet: Yesterday, Google started rolling out its Universal Cart, and the company is very prominently placing it in Search, AI Mode, Chrome, and the Gemini app. more…
fullText:
Yesterday, Google started rolling out its Universal Cart, and the company is very prominently placing it in Search, AI Mode, Chrome, and the Gemini app.

This “intelligent shopping cart” was previewed in May at I/O 2026 as a “hub for shopping on Google.” It’s meant to help “organize your shopping, keep track of items you love from across retailers, stay on top of promos, and enjoy effortless checkout powered by the Universal Commerce Protocol.”

Universal Cart is now rolling out in the US, and we’re starting to see it in Google Search. A new shopping cart icon will appear in the top-right corner of google.com’s homepage and Search results, as well as on desktop Chrome’s New Tab Page. Clicking slides out a panel with two tabs for “Cart” and “My orders.” 

On mobile, the shopping cart appears to the left of the profile switcher in the Google app for Android. That icon also appears on the AI Mode homepage. 

	

In the Gemini app, “Cart and orders” now appears in the account menu.

This Universal Cart icon might be too prominent. It makes Google Search results that have nothing to do with purchases feel like a store page. This is incredibly jarring the first time you see it.

Google product pages gain an “Add to cart” button, with the Universal Cart letting you save products from multiple retailers. A pretty useful capability will automatically keep track of availability changes while offering price drop notifications. 

When you’re ready to purchase, Universal Cart will surface promo codes and highlight which payment method in Google Wallet will give you the most perks. Stores like Nike, Target, Walmart, and Shopify merchants will let you make purchases right from the Google interface.

title: WhatsApp may soon let iPhone users open any link in an in-app browser
snippet: After introducing limited in-app browser support for certain business links last year, WhatsApp is now working on expanding the feature to all links shared in chats. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After introducing limited in-app browser support for certain business links last year, WhatsApp is now working on expanding the feature to all links shared in chats. Here are the details.

WhatsApp working on optional in-app browser

Last May, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp had begun testing a feature that would allow “users to view certain HTTPS-secured business sites within the app,” with the option to open those links in their default browser via the three-dot menu.

Now, the site reports that WhatsApp is working on extending this support to all in-chat links.

Although the feature is not yet available to beta testers, WABetaInfo has uncovered references to it in the latest TestFlight build and shared screenshots showing how it will work.

According to the site, a new “In-app browser” option under Settings > Chats will let users choose whether links open directly within WhatsApp or in their default browser.

Image: WABetaInfo

The same settings screen will also let users clear cookies, cache, and other browsing data stored by WhatsApp’s in-app browser.

	

Here’s WABetaInfo:

Users will be able to enable the in-app browser from the app settings. Here, WhatsApp will add a new option called “In-app browser”. When users enable this feature, they will be able to open any link they send and receive in the chat screen. When users enable this option for the first time, WhatsApp will show a bottom sheet that explains how the feature works. It informs users that they can now open any link within WhatsApp rather than in the default browser. Users will be able to restore the default browser at any time.

The report notes that “WhatsApp cannot see links shared in the conversation and which ones users open.”

As is usually the case with references discovered in WhatsApp’s TestFlight builds, there is currently no word on when the app plans to make the feature available to beta testers or the general public.

title: Gurman: iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID are already being tested inside Apple
snippet: The iPhone Duo comes out tomorrow but, given the strong pre-order demand, it is already looking to be a smash hit. fullText:
The iPhone Duo comes out tomorrow but, given the strong pre-order demand, it is already looking to be a smash hit. And we are all expecting Apple to follow up with a second-generation model next fall, which means the company has to be already working on the next-gen hardware.

On his Power On podcast, Mark Gurman reports that iPhone Duo 2 prototypes inside Apple include Face ID, with the Face ID sensor being integrated beneath the display on the outer screen.

The shift from Face ID to Touch ID on this phone was one of the biggest complaints raised by early iPhone Duo reviewers. 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller called it “the hardest thing to get used to” with the new foldable.

For the first-gen iPhone Duo, fitting Face ID inside the super-thin enclosure seemed to be the blocker. But Apple has been working on making Face ID smaller and less obtrusive, as seen with the under-display IR camera on the iPhone 18 Pro. 

With iPhone Duo 2 and the twentieth anniversary iPhone Pro, we may see another evolution where both the IR camera and the flood illuminator go behind the screen, allowing the bezel or Dynamic Island cutout to be even smaller still.

	

Obviously, that just because they are testing the technology on iPhone Duo prototypes right now, it is not guaranteed that it will ship in next year’s revision. But it seems like that is what Apple is aiming for, so customers can probably expect it either next year or as part of the iPhone Duo 3, if development slips. 

On the same episode, Gurman also says that employees have been exploring ways to also bring the Action button to a next-generation model of iPhone Duo as well, although he seems less confident about this.

It’s also unclear if Apple would remove the Touch ID sensor from the power button if it adds Face ID to the device, or whether it would keep both methods of biometrics allowing users to authenticate whether they are looking at the inner or outer display.

title: Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports
snippet: After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports. more…
fullText:
After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports.

On the homepage, you’ll see a notification bell icon next to the profile switcher in the top-right corner. Tapping opens a feed with “updates about items in Wallet.” 

Earlier this month, the company said it was introducing an “in-app message center in Google Wallet.” This new feature is still rolling out via a server-side update.

Meanwhile, Google Wallet is adding support for more digital passports. Officially referred to as an “ID pass” in the app, usage varies by country. US passports can be used at TSA security via NFC or QR code scanning. 

	

Following Brazil, Singapore, Taiwan, United Kingdom, and the United States of America, we’re starting to see the ability to add Ireland and Italy.

The new countries are not widely rolled out yet.

To add a passport, tap the ‘plus’ FAB at the bottom of Google Wallet > IDs & personal info > ID pass. The registration process involves scanning your passport info page and security chip. Afterward, you have to record a video of your face. You’ll get a notification once verification is complete.

title: Google reiterates missing Fitbit Air sleep breathing quality feature coming ‘soon’
snippet: Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month. more…
fullText:
Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month.

Under the Your Health Guardian umbrella of features, Google recently announced several new features for its fitness trackers. That includes not only the Pixel Watch series, but the Fitbit Air and even the newly announced Fitbit Edge. That suite provides access to blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality. 

The Fitbit Air has been left without one of these features since Google announced them – sleep breathing quality. Google recently stated, once again, that the Fitbit Air would get the features soon in a statement to Android Authority, this time more pointedly aimed at the missing function.

Sleep Breathing Quality launched first on Pixel Watches and will come to Fitbit Air soon.

When Google first announced these features, they made sure to include that detail in the press release so as not to get Fitbit Air users’ hopes up. At the time, Google said sleep breathing quality and other features in the Your Health Guardian suite would be added to the screenless tracker “later this year.” It didn’t note that only two of the three features would be released for the Fitbit Air.

	

That being said, neither the comment nor the original press release lays out a detailed timeline for sleep breathing quality trends, specifically. For now, the Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4, and Pixel Watch 5 are able to set sleep quality, insulin trends, and blood pressure trends on their devices with the Health Guardian feature.

Fitbit Air users will need to wait a little longer.

title: The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say
snippet: Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables. more…
fullText:
Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables.

Samsung provides display panels for both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, both of which have gained a massive amount of attention in the last couple of months. That’s credited to the form factor – a refreshing change from the tall and narrow Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or the devices that emulate the same experience.

Analysts at Omdia reported their forecast for 2026 in the wake of renewed interest in foldables, driven by Samsung and Apple. The report states that foldable AMOLED display shipments are expected to increase by 44% year-over-year. That includes shipments for any foldable displays, but it’s signaled by the surge of wide foldables released or rumored this year.

That increase would be driven by Samsung, if the prediction plays out perfectly. Samsung currently holds a majority lead in foldable display shipments, but it’s possible its slice grows to 66% in 2026. Omdia predicts that current Chinese manufacturers with high shipments will see a decline as demand from Apple and Samsung grows.

	

It’s unlikely we’ll see Samsung and Apple dominate the wide fold market. Motorola is expected to launch a similar foldable, and more will chase the size and shape Apple landed on for its first foldable iPhone.

It sounds like for anyone who struggles to reach interface elements along the left or right edge of the device, iPhone Duo’s forthcoming Reachability feature should help.

fullText:
We’re just a week away from the official announcement of the first ever touchscreen Mac. The upcoming MacBook Pro will also have an OLED screen, which may include a Dynamic Island, and is said to be lighter. 

We don’t yet know the price of the new model, but we can be sure it will carry a significant premium over the existing one. My guess would be somewhere in the $500 to $700 range …

There’s so far been a fair degree of excitement about an OLED Mac. In some ways that’s certainly justified given the quality of the OLED screens we’ve seen on the iPad Pro. On the other hand, Apple’s IPS LCD panels with mini-LED backlighting have always looked fantastic, and I would say rival many competing OLED screens. For that reason, I’m expecting the improvement in display quality to be rather modest.

	

I’ve seen way less interest in the touchscreen. While there is certainly a segment of Apple fans who are eagerly awaiting it, the majority view seems to be that it will have limited utility and be a fingerprint magnet. My own experience of using a 12.9in iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard as a pseudo laptop is that I used the trackpad for everything except scrolling, so I don’t personally see much appeal in a touchscreen Mac.

A lighter MacBook is always welcome, of course, and if the weight difference is significant, that may be a reason to consider it. But unless it’s going to get somewhere close to the weight of a MacBook Air, it’s perhaps not worth such a substantial premium.

Assuming I’m right about the price premium, you’ll be paying somewhere in the region of $600 more for the new machine. For that much, you could double the RAM or double the size of your SSD when buying the existing model. Which would you consider the better deal?

title: People are vibe coding their way to better TVs
snippet: Just imagine… a nice, clean homescreen with no ads, thanks to Claude. | Image: cleanyourtv Vibe coding has reached TVs. Social media is awash with posts from people using LLMs and open-source tools to remove ads and tracking, trim bloat so the OS runs faster, and even completely change the look and organization of their homescreens. While a lot of it is fun - one user turned their TV homescreen into a Pokémon town - I think there's a level of frustration behind it, too. And TV companies should take notice. Vibe coded my parents' TV this afternoon! It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix. Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher. Looks … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Vibe coding has reached TVs. Social media is awash with posts from people using LLMs and open-source tools to remove ads and tracking, trim bloat so the OS runs faster, and even completely change the look and organization of their homescreens. While a lot of it is fun — one user turned their TV homescreen into a Pokémon town — I think there’s a level of frustration behind it, too. And TV companies should take notice.

Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox, and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things — remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you’re watching — without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV’s built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokémon one below.

Most of the projects we’ve seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don’t require root access or firmware hacking, and they’re reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android’s ability to install custom launchers — in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.

As Verge friend Chris Person notes in his Aftermath post, none of this requires AI. These projects take advantage of capabilities that already exist in Android, and in some cases reinvent the wheel. Android debloating programs that use ADB have been around for years, and so have replacement launchers that make Google TV OS look like Apple TV. AI just made the process easier and faster.

There’s nothing similar available for Samsung’s Tizen OS or LG’s webOS, apart from rooting the TV, which is a whole different level of hacking and device control. While there’s a webOS vibe hack for LG TVs that’s based on cleanyourtv, it doesn’t really do the same thing, essentially streaming the Apple TV-like launcher from an always-on device on the same network. They also won’t work for Roku or Vizio’s SmartCast.

These projects, or any OS vibe coding someone might attempt, won’t necessarily stop all data collection. A good basic rule is that if the TV is connected to the internet, it’s collected at least some data. Dumbtv blocks certain manufacturer and ad partner addresses your TV sends data to, but since it’s usually encrypted during transit, knowing what exactly gets sent is impossible. The data blocking is similar to what you can do with Pi-hole to block malicious DNS requests on your network.

TVs have increasingly become a means for companies to gather viewing data and serve up ads. By using automatic content recognition (ACR) and digital fingerprinting, manufacturers are able to know what content you’re watching, send that information to their ad partners, and then display targeted ads on the TV.

ACR isn’t just used for ads, though. It allows companies to measure audience metrics, and it can feed show recommendations based on what you’ve watched. It’s important to note that users need to agree to ACR tracking, and there are ways to opt out of it after the fact in a TV’s menus (although those options are not always easy to find). There are also options in most menus — again, usually buried — for turning off targeted ads.

But even after doing that, there’s always concern that companies still collect some amount of your data and use it in ways you might not be comfortable with. Whether or not it’s true does little to assuage those fears. The weekend of vibe coding, on the other hand, is a way for people to try and take control of their TVs to get the user experience they want.

There are also dangers to vibe-coding your TV. One person who tried to vibe-hack a Samsung TV with Claude bricked it. The only way to fully avoid ACR, ads, or any type of data collection is to never connect it to the internet. A firmware download to a USB stick can apply critical updates instead of Wi-Fi or Ethernet. If you still want to stream content, a streaming device that doesn’t use ACR, like an Apple TV 4K (grab a last-generation model before the expensive new one replaces it), is an option. But any streaming requires sharing some amount of your data with someone to function properly.

The biggest takeaway from the vibe-coding weekend is that the current state of TV OSes has people fed up. Most people aren’t going to stop watching TV anytime soon, but the experience needs to improve. The ads, the data collection, and the cluttered layouts are too aggravating. AI now allows anyone to code their own solution, and it’s only going to get easier. If TV manufacturers don’t take note and make changes, there’s a chance that users will make the changes for them.

title: The real reason to care about Vivo’s latest phone is the camera [Gallery]
snippet: The Vivo V80 sports flagship design quality, a massive 7200mAh battery, Center-Stage selfie camera, IP68/69 ingress protection, and one of the wildest AI camera modes I’ve seen yet. more…
fullText:
The Vivo V80 sports flagship design quality, a massive 7200mAh battery, Center-Stage selfie camera, IP68/69 ingress protection, and one of the wildest AI camera modes I’ve seen yet.

When I think of the smartphone industry’s best cameras, Vivo or Oppo usually comes to mind. While both companies offer good experiences on any phone they sell, their best features often appear only on flagship models. But the Vivo V80, which retails for just ₹62,999 (~$660), features the company’s new flagship AI camera mode, and that might be the single most interesting thing about the release for me.

Let’s get the full specs out of the way first. The Vivo V80’s got a 6.59-inch 144Hz OLED display, featuring 1.5k resolution, true 10-bit colors (no dithering), and 4320Hz PWM dimming at low brightness (plus an option for full DC dimming). Inside is a Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, 8GB RAM, and that massive 7200mAh battery with 90W charging. Good stuff.

The Vivo V80 uses a main 50MP Sony LYTIA 700V sensor, a 3x optical 50MP Sony IMX882 telephoto camera, an 8MP or 12MP ultrawide camera (region-dependent), and a 50MP ZEISS center-stage 90-degree selfie camera. The phone is available in India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and other regions in the coming weeks.

	

To illustrate just how interesting the new AI Creation camera mode is, I took a bunch of photos using the same mode on the Vivo X500. That phone is about $300 more expensive, but it features the same AI Creation mode as the Vivo V80. The results are nothing short of jaw-dropping at times. Let’s start with the hike I took this weekend.

It was a gorgeous autumn day, but the sporadic cloud cover was really killing the vibe of my photos. The lighting was annoyingly flat, and the colors my eyes were seeing in the leaves weren’t being picked up on camera at all. So I swiped over to the AI Creation mode and hit the shutter button. The rest was all automated.

The amount of depth and color this mode added truly blew my mind. When you open the mode and point the viewfinder toward something, it scans the scene and automatically applies the style it thinks will be best. It’ll also give you two additional modes to quickly select from, or you can jump into the full UI and choose the one you want.

From here, you can also choose to have Vivo’s AI automatically remove anyone in the photo, and it does an impeccable job, too; no circling required! Original images are always available in Vivo’s Albums app, and you can select a different style after taking the photo.

This mode is 100% cloud processing, though, so you might need to wait to see the processing results if you were somewhere like I was with no signal. Processing takes about one minute per photo, and up to 10 images can be processed simultaneously. If there’s a processing limit per day, I didn’t find it. While the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 in the Vivo V80 could probably handle some of the processing, this ensures you get the best quality without much wait time.

The “Travel” category creates genuinely convincing effects like the Sunlight style. Vivo has several other options that are more dramatic and, therefore, obviously edited-looking. In the header image, I grabbed one of my son’s swords and asked him to take a picture of me. The sword and the room are fully real in these pictures, but the lighting and effects are all automatically generated by Vivo.

All of these, too, were quite convincing, despite obviously being stylized. I particularly love the mist one, although I’m not sure how often anyone would use most of these. They’re clearly only for niche dramatic photos, but hey, maybe you love that sort of thing. The rest of the options available under the “Landscape” category were initially convincing, but zooming in just a bit reveals some very obvious AI editing.

So all of this is amazing, but there’s one big problem that I’m not thrilled about: Vivo doesn’t use SynthID or another more standardized way of noting that these images are edited with AI. If you delve into the EXIF data, you can find “ai_creation” in the comments field, but Gemini apparently isn’t smart enough to understand that yet.

Most likely, Gemini and the rest will figure this out in time, but I don’t care much for AI editing tools that don’t automatically mark them as such. Vivo, if you’re reading this, please add SynthID or another way for AI tools to identify these as automated. Otherwise, this is a dope mode that I love seeing proliferate to more affordable phones like the Vivo V80, especially in the age of RAMageddon.

title: Google explains how to fix time zones on Android amid changes in Canada
snippet: As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone. more…
fullText:
As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone.

When Daylight Saving Time comes to an end next month, parts of Canada will not be rolling back their clocks as the time change becomes permanent. Manitoba announced the change in September, with other parts of the country, including Alberta and British Columbia, also no longer changing their times twice a year, but different provinces and territories are making their own choices regarding which time to stick with.

Google, in a post, subtly acknowledges that things could get a little messy with these time zone changes and your Android phone.

Time is usually set automatically on Android, and it sounds like that will still happen for the most part. Google says to “apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device” if your phone’s time is incorrect on November 1 after the changes kick in.

	

But if there are still problems, you can make adjustments in the Settings of your Android device:

If you are still seeing an incorrect time or time zone, you can enable location-based time zone detection:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Enable “Automatic time zone”.

Enable “Use location for time zone”.

or set the time zone manually:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Disable “Automatic time zone”.

Choose “Time Zone”.

Choose “Region”.

Choose “Canada”.

Choose a time zone with the right offset.

title: TextNow’s $150 Yello Phone Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
snippet: The lower-cost phone has a parent portal for managing calls and texts, checking the phone’s location, and enabling games.
fullText:
Low-cost carrier TextNow launched its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized 2024 edition of the Moto G Play that costs $150 and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments. It’s a simple 4G-only Android phone with a 6.5-inch display, but TextNow makes a number of software changes to restrict most access to the internet.

The phone doesn’t include Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

			

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts.TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 50-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2024 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. Its 5,000-mAh battery should easily get through a day or two of use, and its IP52 certification should keep it resistant to light splashes of water. The phone has a limited amount of storage at 64GB, but that might work out fine considering the deliberate constraints placed on this device.

It’s worth noting that Motorola is only providing security support to this older model of the Moto G Play through 2027, but TextNow’s website says that its Yello software will continue to be built upon as the carrier gets user feedback. Since Motorola’s official support period for this phone is almost over, it will be important for TextNow’s Yello software to step in as it builds up features for this phone for kids.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same sapphire blue that’s on every 2024 Moto G Play.

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited that Yello was using a different edition of the Moto G Play. TextNow clarified the model after Yello’s announcement, and the story has been updated accordingly.

title: The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
snippet: An Xbox Elite controller. | Photo by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication's Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028. My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It's DOA. My second thought: Microsoft knows people won't pay that much. It couldn't possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. "I wouldn't release it at all," former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said. My third thought: Didn't Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won't pay that much? Didn't old Xbox boss Phil Spencer say "We're no … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication’s Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028.

My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It’s DOA.

My second thought: Microsoft knows people won’t pay that much. It couldn’t possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. “I wouldn’t release it at all,” former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said.

My third thought: Didn’t Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won’t pay that much?

Didn’t old Xbox boss Phil Spencer say “We’re not going to grow the market with $1,000 consoles”?

Didn’t new Xbox boss Asha Sharma say “We’ve reached a point where it will be hard to imagine that mass audiences can afford thousands of dollars to spend” on a box?

Didn’t Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball say the entire company would change its practices to make sure it’s affordable?

Didn’t Sharma say Xbox would need to adopt “radically different business models” to keep Xbox from being too pricey?

Did Fortune get it wrong?

I don’t think Fortune’s insiders are the problem here. With today’s incredibly overpriced RAM and storage, it wouldn’t be surprising if it cost over a thousand dollars to build, package, distribute, and sell “the largest technical leap you will have ever seen in a hardware generation,” as former Xbox president Sarah Bond called the next Xbox back in 2024.

But there are at least five ways the report could be correct without making you pay all that money at once. I just don’t think you’re going to like most of them.

Subsidies: Microsoft could pay to give you a discount

The least-likely possibility is the one Fortune suggests itself. Let’s look at the original quote, bolding mine:

[…] the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.

Historically, Microsoft has subsidized the Xbox. Microsoft sold boxes at a loss right out of the gate, making its profits when you buy games and Xbox Game Pass subscriptions instead of on the hardware alone. That’s not our speculation — it’s exactly what Microsoft told The Verge in 2021. In 2023, we learned that Microsoft may have spent $1.5 billion to make sure it could sell the Xbox Series X and S at $499 and $299 respectively, instead of what they actually cost.

But Microsoft has suggested that it’s done with hardware subsidies. “Going forward, this cannot continue,” wrote Sharma in her “Xbox reset” memo, referring to the $20 billion in content, platform, and hardware subsidies Microsoft made over the past five years.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that idea on the Hard Fork podcast: “No one can accuse Microsoft of not having invested for the last 25 years, and now we have to turn this into a sustainable business.”

It isn’t just new management that’s hinting at no more subsidies: Bond primed the pump for a $1,000 box when she called Helix “a very premium, very high-end curated experience” late last year, comparing it to gaming PCs like the $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld.

Perhaps Microsoft has changed its mind since then. “We are working very hard to rethink everything that we can about Helix,” Ball said in June, referring to affordability. “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan,” Sharma said in February (though not about affordability specifically).

But subsidies would be a tremendous risk if the Helix still plays PC games in addition to Xbox ones. Valve’s Steam is by far the dominant PC gaming platform — so PC gamers who buy a Helix won’t help Microsoft recoup its money.

Subscription: “Get it free with 36 months of Xbox Game Pass and qualifying trade-in”

There’s another way Microsoft could subsidize a $1,200 Xbox.

Today, AT&T will give you a $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro for $0* — if you lock yourself into 36 months of AT&T phone service that costs $100 or more per month and trade in a recent phone, too.

Microsoft could do the same with a new, pricier tier of its Xbox Game Pass game subscription service, effectively bundling the games with the console and making you slowly pay for both at the same time. Perhaps you’ll have the option to buy an “unlocked” Xbox for full price, but it won’t be the norm.

To make it happen directly, Microsoft would need a pricier new tier of Xbox Game Pass, which wouldn’t necessarily align with the company’s recent moves. Sharma actually cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate to $22.99 a month in April, writing that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players,” while removing Call of Duty games and unlimited access to Xbox Cloud Gaming from the deal.

I don’t know if it would work. People feel naked leaving the house without phone service. They might not feel the same about games. Subscription fatigue is real. But if it worked, Microsoft’s moat would be stronger than ever. You’ll be more likely to play the games you’ve already paid for and are committed to keep paying for. Many would get sucked into a profitable upgrade cycle, just like they do with phones, since they can buy the next Xbox for “$0” as soon as it comes out.

Cellphone subsidies have been around nearly as long as pricey phones: The 1994 IBM Simon, arguably the first smartphone, eventually cost half its $1,100 price tag if you signed a contract with BellSouth. My first phone, a Kyocera QCP-6035 with a built-in PalmPilot, was subsidized when it arrived in 2001. So it’s not exactly a “radical new business model,” but it would be new for game consoles.

Rental: Maybe most people won’t own a Helix themselves

It’s also possible that Microsoft simply doesn’t plan to sell a console to the masses anymore — it can sell an $1,800 Xbox to those who can afford “video game ownership” and try to hook everyone else on the Netflix model.

After all, the “K-shaped economy” and RAMageddon have already made gaming PCs and existing game consoles into luxury goods. Society’s wealthier individuals seem perfectly happy to pay inflated prices for the few consoles Sony and Microsoft still pump out.

While PS5 sales plummeted after Sony’s price hikes, that may have been about component shortages rather than decreased demand. Xbox sales reportedly rose over a similar period, and Microsoft has justified repeated, dramatic price hikes on its consoles since May 2025.

“I can tell you definitively, demand for our console exceeds supply. We are putting them in as many stores as possible, we are producing them as quickly as possible. There is a severe limitation to how quickly we can do that,” Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball told The Game Business in June, blaming RAM shortages.

But Microsoft has another way of giving less affluent people access to “next-gen” Xbox power. It can rent you one. The company just launched pay-as-you-go cloud gaming starting at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud gaming (50 hours for $11.99).

Maybe all of Microsoft’s recent talk about affordability isn’t about the masses owning a next-gen console. Maybe it’s about finding an affordable way for people to “play Xbox” without owning the games at all.

The next gen is the current gen

After Fortune’s report, some of the very first reactions I saw boiled down to this: “I’m out. Forget next gen, I’m going to stick with my existing Xbox/PlayStation/Switch.”

That’ll be the reality for many people if the Xbox costs over a thousand bucks. But if the RAM shortage continues — if Microsoft knows it’ll sell every Xbox it can make to wealthy individuals because it can’t make a lot — it’s not necessarily a huge risk to sell it sky-high on day one.

Perhaps the Xbox Helix will be an early adopter console, the same way the iPhone Duo is an early adopter phone, the same way the Steam Frame is an early adopter headset. These products are selling out instantly despite their high price tags, leaving many would-be buyers in the cold. They’re shipping messy and unfinished, but that’s okay because early adopters want to come along for the ride.

Microsoft knows the same is true of some Xbox buyers, because it helped ship an unfinished $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld even before the RAM crisis, and the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 follow-up is already sold out.

But if Microsoft splits the Xbox audience into “have” and “have-not,” it means the next generation won’t truly arrive. Game developers won’t spend all their effort targeting a console people can’t buy. The next Xbox won’t be any more necessary than a PS5 Pro if you already own a PS5. In industry lingo, the Helix would be a “mid-cycle refresh” instead of true next gen.

I wouldn’t hate that, though, and neither would many video game execs. They’ve long complained that the pace of technology has ballooned the cost of building a video game to unsustainable levels, leading to today’s world where too many development teams are cut to the bone right after their games ship.

Former PlayStation and Xbox execs like Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden, and Mike Ybarra have argued that the next gen isn’t necessary.

“Stick with PS5 Pro/Series X until prices normalize. The capabilities of those boxes are both fine for 99% of the audience. No one is screaming ‘I need a more powerful console’ right now,” Ybarra tweeted on October 20th.

“I think [Sony and Nintendo] should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because I think people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2,” Yoshida told me on The Vergecast.

“I think we’ve plateaued on the tech, frankly,” Layden told GamesIndustry.biz in 2025. (He’s said similar before and since.) “Make it cheaper and simpler. Let’s do that instead. And let’s find a way to have more hardware companies participate.”

Microsoft and its chip partner AMD have already taken one step to help extend the current generation — AMD’s performance-enhancing FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series S and X, which should make it easier for both to deliver crisp 4K images to your TV.

Pay what you can afford

Even if Microsoft ships a $1,800 console, the company’s been clear it won’t be the only Xbox you can buy. Sharma has publicly said that Helix will be a “family of devices,” which has been broadly interpreted to mean that Microsoft will let PC industry partners like Asus sell their own “Xbox” as well.

If the reporting pans out, that wouldn’t just be a cobranded Xbox Ally handheld that runs Windows — Asus could make a console-shaped box that runs a Windows-based Xbox OS, too.

Some of those partners could offer more affordable, less powerful Xboxes than Microsoft’s own flagship box, perhaps with less storage and memory. Microsoft, too, might have creative solutions for storage, like how the company shipped the Xbox 360 with different-size hard drives, or none at all, to make it more affordable. “We will have to empower customers to have very flexible storage offerings,” Sharma said in June.

Or you could buy another Xbox that’s likely going to continue to count as part of Microsoft’s “family”: the existing Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.

This can all work because games don’t need to target a single console anymore; they haven’t needed to for a long time. An Xbox One game runs on an Xbox One X and an Xbox Series S and an Xbox Series X because they’re all effectively AMD-powered Windows PCs, just with different amounts of performance on tap. The Xbox Helix is a powerful extension of the same continuum. The same is true of PlayStation 4, PS4 Pro, PS5, PS5 Pro, and presumably PS6, minus the Windows part.

Perhaps a particular piece of hardware will stand out as the one developers should target as the baseline for “it looks and runs great on Xbox,” the same way the Steam Deck handheld became a baseline for PC game developers starting in 2022. Maybe, like the Steam Deck and the Nintendo Switch, it’ll help reset our expectations of what a top-shelf game needs to look like.

At this rate, I wouldn’t be surprised if the existing Xbox Series S will be the one. But it could also be Microsoft’s own next handheld Xbox. Fortune’s insiders say it’s coming holiday 2027.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Sean Hollister

title: Modretro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it?
snippet: As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways. more…
fullText:
As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways.

I have a decent number of original gaming consoles from the 90s, but the Game Boy is arguably the handheld that I covet the most. I was a little too young to really enjoy the DMG model, but the Game Boy Color was the first EDC I ever owned. It still has a special place in my heart that very few things can match.

Luckily for me, my parents didn’t throw my original clear “Atomic Purple” Game Boy Color away under the guise of ditching clutter at home. It’s a piece of art, one that I love dearly, but it’s missing out on the fundamentals of a good gadget by 2026 standards.

Using original hardware isn’t always ideal. You miss out on a backlit display, the battery longevity is often subpar, and, in the interests of hardware preservation, I don’t want to break something that means so much to me.

	

That’s kind of why I picked up the original Modretro Chromatic last year. That is a high-end FPGA Game Boy clone that replicates software emulation with hardware-level logic recreation. You’re able to play original cartridges with supremely accurate visuals, sounds, timing, all that good stuff.

The original Chromatic was kind of pricey at over $200 with the Sapphire glass display and all-metal chassis. Sure, those are “nice-to-haves,” but the new Modretro Chromatic Transparent lowers the price of entry and adds back in the transparent tech highlight of my youth for under $150 – with a copy of Tetris. Maybe you need to be a 90s kid to truly understand the appeal. I’m just glad that brands are at least offering us these kinds of options again.

I’ve been carrying this thing for a few weeks in my sidebag in place of my orange Chromatic, and it’s a different beast in many ways. Being able to play all of my favorite Game Boy games isn’t anything new, and sure, I could use an emulator on my phone, but there’s nothing quite like playing as Nintendo intended.

From a purely holistic standpoint, you’re going back to the slow, intentional gaming that is completely vanilla. Mod-free, methodical gaming that feels intentional. I love emulation as much as anyone, but playing at 1x speed rather than trying to speedrun the grinding of Pokémon is a throwback.

Okay, it’s not a gadget for everyone. It’s more of a fancy thing that old heads will adore because it literally does one thing exceptionally well. The screen is 1:1, and includes the all-important backlighting. It does downgrade the scratch protection to Gorilla Glass, but that is far better than what the original Game Boy could ever claim.

By default, it takes three AA batteries, or you can pick up a rechargeable battery pack that charges up through the USB-C port. The port does a little more, like letting you stream to Discord and update on-device firmware. Make no mistake, the Chromatic Transparent is made for the modern era, despite doing one thing and one thing only.

I was sent the green Chromatic Clear, and it’s almost jewel-like, which demands attention. I like that it isn’t quite neon; the smoky color feels premium despite the material difference from the original Chromatic. It will pick up scuffs and dings. Personally, I see that as a patina that means I’m playing my favorite games, which, in my opinion, we should all do more of. Although some of my original carts need battery replacements, I’m using a flash cart to play through my collection.

The buttons are not quite 1:1 with the original Game Boy Color. I’d say they’re a little “stiffer” but feel about as close as you could get without being outright replicas. I know some people won’t like the D-pad. It’s marginally harder to roll through the four directions than an actual Game Boy, so some games may play a little differently.

My only major criticism is that the volume scroll wheel is too easy to adjust without intent. So be aware that you might inadvertently increase the volume while launching the Modretro settings menu.

On that, the speaker is a solitary downward-firing mono speaker, and it gets loud with no distortion. It’s amazing to hear the earworm of the Tetris theme playing at full blast, but remember to tone the volume down when you’re in public.

For anyone wondering why you wouldn’t use an original Game Boy Color to play your games, well, that’s a very fair comment. However, to get a modded Game Boy Color that has all the same functionality, it actually costs upwards of $150 from most reputable sellers on sites like eBay. Modretro is basically undercutting the original with lots of quality-of-life changes with the Chromatic Transparent.

As much as I love this hardware and will covet it in my EDC, you simply cannot separate the company from the controversial founder, Palmer Luckey. To many, the ties to his business ventures outside the gaming space will tarnish the brand. I can understand hesitation, and while I was sent this device for review, you will need to decide for yourself if you are willing to support the company. It would be unfair to omit this; hence, mentioning it.

It would also be a lie if I were not to say I’m smitten with the product. I do wish it were not marked with this extra controversy, as it’s the best way for ardent retro gamers to play through your back catalog of Game Boy titles.

For $150, the Chromatic Transparent is not a cheap way to indulge in some nostalgia. However, it’s undercutting the competition and now has even better colors to choose from.

title: iPhone Duo orders limited to two per customer as Apple tackles scalping
snippet: Apple is limiting iPhone Duo orders to a maximum of two per customer in the US, UK, and elsewhere after shipping dates slipped into January of next year within minutes of pre-orders opening. The move appears to be an attempt to tackle the problem of scalping, where people buy large volumes of supply-constrained devices in order to resell them on eBay for well above the retail price … more…
fullText:
Apple is limiting iPhone Duo orders to a maximum of two per customer in the US, UK, and elsewhere after shipping dates slipped into January of next year within minutes of pre-orders opening.

The move appears to be an attempt to tackle the problem of scalping, where people buy large volumes of supply-constrained devices in order to resell them on eBay for well above the retail price …

Engadget reports that it tried to add more than two iPhone Duo units to its cart on the Apple stores in the US, UK, Japan, and Spain, and received a notification advising it of the limit.

We’ve tried adding more than two units to our cart on the Apple Stores for Japan, Spain and the United Kingdom, in addition to the US, and we’ve received a warning notice across all the online stores. The notification said: “A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out.”

The site said that the same limit applies no matter what configuration you select.

The company is almost certainly implementing the move in a bid to reduce scalping. We’ve already seen dozens of iPhone Duos listed on eBay by scalpers, some with prices exceeding $5,000.

It’s not the first time Apple has imposed limits on supply-constrained iPhones. The company has done this in China multiple times, with limits applied to walk-in purchases in retail stores as well as those made online. The company has also done it in the US before, with the first example being the iPhone 5 way back in 2012.

9to5Mac’s Take

Industrial-level scalping is hard to defeat. Organized gangs use multiple virtual credit card numbers, email addresses, and delivery addresses in order to circumvent limits. Others pay people to place orders on their behalf.

All the same, it’s good to see Apple at least attempting to reduce the scale of the problem. It’s also possible the company is implementing other behind-the-scenes measures to detect and reject more sophisticated bulk purchase attempts.

As we predicted, some customers have seen improvements to their estimated delivery dates. It’s also worth trying for a walk-in purchase if you live close to an Apple store – just not on day one.

title: FTC Imposter Scam Threatens to Unplug Your Phone Number
snippet: Trust this genuine FTC warning. And maybe just don’t answer your phone.
fullText:
The scam du jour sounds like a real brain twister. According to a Federal Trade Commission alert issued Thursday about the newest imposter scam, fraudsters pretending to be from the FTC are calling to “warn” you that your phone number is being used to commit scams in another country and that if you don’t reply to them ASAP you run the risk of your phone getting deactivated. 

And it sounds like a pretty intricate hoax. According to the alert, the caller will transfer you to a phony police officer and provide a search query to find the (fake) phone number to file a “report,” and if you call, more scammers pick up. And once you’ve handed over your personal information, they’ll tell you you have to travel to the relevant country to resolve it, unless you fork over a “security deposit.”

This is just one of the latest in the raft of scams we face daily, and frequently fall for. I know the recents list on my phone is mostly pages and pages of suspected-spam-labeled calls.

			

More from CNET

Just picking up provides scammers with the knowledge that your phone number is active and that you may be more likely to fall for the next step down a fraud’s path. Answering adds value to your personal information and a link to it all in its own.

I think scams like these rely on a series of adrenaline-fueled responses — the little spikes you get when you hear the phone ring, then see the ID (it’s the government!) and, if you pick up, the succession of scary warnings. Ignoring unexpected calls from strangers gives you time to think rationally about claims, if they leave a voicemail, and if they don’t, that’s telling as well. 

In this case, it could start with the realization that it’s truly unlikely the FTC would be contacting individuals about this, especially before issuing a public statement that there’s a problem.

title: Soon You Won’t Have to Do Dishes at an Airbnb (Unless You Really Want To)
snippet: The lodging platform is updating its policies around what hosts can require of guests.
fullText:
You’re checking out in an hour, and there’s a pile of dishes. If it’s an Airbnb, don’t worry about it. The lodging platform recently updated its policy about what hosts can ask guests to do, and some cleaning chores are now off the list.

In the Reasonable House Rules and requests page on its website, Airbnb says hosts cannot “ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

Airbnb said there could be exceptions — “We understand every home is unique” — such as asking guests to limit water use if there are local restrictions due to drought, or to put trash in a bear-proof container at a woodsy lodging.

			

More from CNET

The app said the new regulations will apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20.

When laying out house rules and guest requests, many hosts require or ask guests to either clean dishes or put them in the dishwasher and run it. They may also ask guests to bag garbage and recyclables, place them in containers outside, and remove sheets and pillowcases from beds and towels from bathrooms, then pile them up for the cleaners.

Some hosts clapped back at the updated policy on the app’s community forum page. René, a host in Berlin, posted, “Seven days of dirty dishes covered in leftover food. Sugar ants and other pests have moved in. The guests check out. But will the pests check out too?” San Francisco host Adam said he would have to raise his cleaning fee by 30 to 50%, and Michelle in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, commented that “the burden of cost has been switched to the hosts.”

Read more: 9 Security Steps I Recommend When You Pull Up to a Vacation Rental

The updated policy is the latest evolution in what has been one of the main complaints about Airbnb — cleaning fees and requirements. In November 2022, Airbnb changed its app and website so that guests could see cleaning and service fees when searching listings. There was a “Display total price” toggle near the top of a search results page that let you see prices that included all fees (but not taxes).

It was a response to years of complaints that listings did not include those fees upfront, in effect masking the true cost of a rental. For example, you go for a lodging at $100 per night, but in the final stages of making your payment, find out it’s actually $200 per night with all the fees included.

Then, in April 2025, Airbnb mandated that all listings worldwide must have the total price upfront, including all fees but not taxes, saying, “We know that clear, upfront pricing improves the Airbnb experience for both guests and hosts.”

Airbnb, which launched in 2008, says it has 5.5 million hosts globally who have served 2.5 billion guest arrivals in nearly every country for all types of lodgings — mansions, cottages, cabins, RVs, teepees, whatever. The platform’s competitors include Vrbo, Booking.com, Expedia and HomeToGo.

Host sees ‘both sides’ of it

Sam Eitzen, CEO and co-founder of experiential marketing platform Snapbar, operates a guest house in Washington listed on Airbnb where I stayed recently (yes, I did the dishes). He said he understands both sides of the issue — as a host and as a guest himself.

“I have been at Airbnbs that make the checkout instructions almost scary, and you worry about getting things wrong,” Eitzen told me. “We’ve never wanted to create that experience and treat the list of ‘chores’ as optional and helpful, but aim to never make guests feel worried about the process or make it sound like we’d come after them or charge them if they don’t.”

Eitzen said Airbnb is “walking a tightrope” in trying to please both hosts and guests. He said the new policy could create confusion, however.

“People will still post rules, lists and manuals in their Airbnbs, and those will most likely conflict with the app, and I think that runs the risk of confusing guests,” he said.

MacBook Pro redesign with OLED, touchscreen, Dynamic Island, more

Apple has a new MacBook Pro coming next week that’s expected to be the star of the ‘Pro and tell’ event. Rumored features include:

Industrial redesign that’s much lighter and slightly thinner

OLED display

Touchscreen

M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

No notch, just a hole-punch camera cutout and Dynamic Island

Similar to how Apple introduced a new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 last fall, we’re expecting an update to that entry model that doesn’t change much besides the M6 chip.
